summary: Sticky assignors assign partitions twice or fail when a member owns a partition that no longer exists
body:
When the leader of a classic consumer group computes the assignment with the StickyAssignor or the CooperativeStickyAssignor, the assignor keeps each partition that a member reports as owned if the partition's topic is in the leader's metadata. It doesn't check the partition number. After a topic is deleted and created again with fewer partitions, a member can report a partition that no longer exists, for example T-3 when T now has 2 partitions.

AbstractStickyAssignor computes the unassigned partitions by walking the sorted owned partitions alongside the sorted partitions of the subscribed topics, and it expects every owned partition to be among them. The walk never gets past an owned partition that no longer exists, so every owned partition sorted after it also counts as unassigned and is assigned a second time.

Impact:
* A partition is assigned to two members, and both consume it.
* A member is assigned a partition that doesn't exist, or the same partition twice.
* When all members subscribe to the same topics, the assignment can fail with IllegalStateException: "No more unfilled consumers to be assigned." The leader's poll() throws it, and the following rebalances fail the same way while members still report the partition.

A member reports such a partition, for example, when the topic is deleted and created again between two metadata refreshes of the leader. The leader sees the partition count drop and triggers a rebalance. Cooperative members still own the old partitions, because they revoke only the partitions of topics that they no longer subscribe to. Eager members revoke all their partitions before they rejoin, but the user data of the StickyAssignor still lists them.

The RangeAssignor and the RoundRobinAssignor don't use the owned partitions and aren't affected.

*Steps to reproduce*
# Call CooperativeStickyAssignor#assign with topic a with 1 partition and topic b with 4 partitions, and two members in generation 1 subscribed to a and b: C1 owns a-0, b-0 and b-2, and C2 owns a-1, b-1 and b-3.
# The assignment fails with IllegalStateException: "No more unfilled consumers to be assigned."

With two more members C3 and C4 that own nothing, the same call returns {C1=[a-0, b-0], C2=[a-1], C3=[b-0], C4=[]}: b-0 goes to C1 and C3, and C2 gets a-1, which doesn't exist.

With topic a with 2 partitions and topic c with 1 partition, C1 subscribed to a and owning a-0 and a-1, and C2 subscribed to a and c and owning c-0 and c-1, the CooperativeStickyAssignor returns {C1=[a-0, a-1, a-0], C2=[c-0, c-1, a-1]}: a-1 goes to C1 and C2, C1 gets a-0 twice, and C2 gets c-1, which doesn't exist. The StickyAssignor returns the same assignment when the owned partitions are in its user data.

*Expected:* the assignors ignore owned partitions that don't exist, assign each partition to one member at most, and don't throw.

summary: ConsumerGroupHeartbeat returns member epoch 0 when a static consumer member replaces a classic member during upgrade of a generation-0 group
body:
When a classic group that has not yet completed its first rebalance (generation 0) is upgraded to a consumer group by a static consumer-protocol member that replaces a classic static member, the ConsumerGroupHeartbeat response returns member epoch 0. Epoch 0 is reserved for members joining a group, so the coordinator must never return it.

KAFKA-20209's assignor offload will widen this bug to all upgrades at generation 0, not just static member replacement upgrades.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Set group.consumer.migration.policy to upgrade, and set group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms high enough that the classic group's initial rebalance doesn't complete during the test.
2. A classic static member with group.instance.id X joins a new group G. The group goes to PreparingRebalance at generation 0 and the JoinGroup stays pending.
3. Before the initial rebalance completes, a consumer-protocol member with a new member id sends ConsumerGroupHeartbeat to G with member epoch 0, instanceId X, and the same subscription as the classic member.
4. The coordinator upgrades G to a consumer group at group epoch 0 and target assignment epoch 0, copied from the classic generation. The consumer member replaces the classic static member and is reset to epoch 0.
5. The subscription is unchanged, so the group epoch isn't bumped. The coordinator considers the target assignment at epoch 0 up to date, and reconciles the new member to epoch 0.
6. The heartbeat response returns member epoch 0.

Expected: the member gets an epoch greater than 0.

—

 

This is a special case of KAFKA-21582.

summary: StackOverflowError in StreamsBuilder.build() for deep processor chains
body: {{StreamsBuilder.build()}} always runs {{NodesWithRelaxedNullKeyJoinDownstream}} (from {{InternalStreamsBuilder.optimizeTopology}} -> {{rewriteRepartitionNodes}}), even with topology optimization disabled. Its {{traverseGraph}} method recurses once per graph node, so the recursion depth equals the length of the longest processor chain. A linear chain of about 8,000 processors (for example repeated {{mapValues}}) throws {{StackOverflowError}} on a default 1 MB thread stack. Replacing the recursion with an iterative traversal fixes it without changing which repartition nodes are rewritten.

summary: CachingKeyValueStore serves a stale value after a read during its own cache flush, so a later read-modify-write silently loses an update
body:
{\{NamedCache#flush}} marks every dirty entry *clean* before the flush listener writes the entries to the underlying store one by one (\{{CachingKeyValueStore#putAndMaybeForward}}). If the stream thread reads the same caching store while that loop is running, a cache miss in \{{CachingKeyValueStore#getInternal}} puts a clean copy into the cache (\{{ThreadCache#put}} -> \{{maybeEvict}}). That can evict entries that are marked clean but *not yet written*; they are dropped silently because they look clean. A later read of such a key misses, loads the *old* value from the underlying store and caches it as clean. The flush loop then writes the *new* value to the underlying store and the changelog, but the cache keeps serving the old value. The next read-modify-write of that key (e.g. a KTable aggregation) builds on the stale value, and the update that was already written is overwritten.

Nothing fails and nothing is logged. The changelog briefly contains the correct value and then a value derived from the older one, so a restored store is wrong as well.

h3. How real topologies reach it
During a flush the listener forwards each entry downstream. Downstream KTable-KTable joins read other caching stores through value getters; their misses evict (the thread cache is shared and full) and can run nested flushes of those stores, whose forwarded entries read the first store again, for other keys. The stack trace in KAFKA-9310 shows this re-entrant path (\{{getInternal}} -> \{{NamedCache.evict}} -> \{{flush}} -> \{{putAndMaybeForward}}) in a real application.

h3. Observed
Kafka Streams 4.2 (Confluent 8.2.1-ce), at_least_once, one stream thread per instance, \{{statestore.cache.max.bytes}} 4 GiB, \{{commit.interval.ms}} 300000. One sub-topology holds ten KTable \{{groupBy().aggregate()}} stores (sets per key) feeding a chain of non-materialized outer joins. During full rebuilds the three largest aggregates (1-1.6 M keys each) lose updates; the small ones never do.

A diagnostic rebuild with repartition purging off and changelog compaction held (so every write stayed visible) lost 44 values on 37 keys of one aggregate. For every one of them: the groupBy record reached the aggregate, the changelog *did* contain a write with the update, and a later write for the same key was computed from the value *before* that write (36 of 37 exactly the previous write). All of them came from one task and one contiguous changelog window (~7,400 writes), written by a cache *eviction* flush (not a commit) in the middle of a burst, during which the same task's sibling stores flushed within the same seconds, one of them without any input of its own (so its flush was triggered by reads). No rebalance, restart, producer error or GC problem.

The bug needs (1) a full thread cache, so that reads during a flush evict, and (2) a stale entry that survives in the cache until the key's next update. That is why it only shows with large stores and large caches, and why small-cache tests do n

summary: Classic group rejects a static member that restarts with GROUP_MAX_SIZE_REACHED when the group is full
body:
When a static member of a classic group restarts, it sends a JoinGroup with its group.instance.id and an empty member id. GroupMetadataManager#classicGroupJoinToClassicGroup calls acceptJoiningMember(group, memberId) before it looks at the instance id, and acceptJoiningMember only checks the member id:
* In Stable and CompletingRebalance, it accepts a member that isn't in the group only if group.numMembers() < group.max.size.
* In PreparingRebalance, it accepts it only if group.numAwaitingJoinResponse() < group.max.size.

So when the group is full, the restarted member is rejected with GROUP_MAX_SIZE_REACHED, although it would replace its old member (classicGroupJoinNewStaticMember) and the group wouldn't grow.

Consumer groups don't have this problem: throwIfConsumerGroupIsFull skips the check when group.hasStaticMember(instanceId), for the ConsumerGroupHeartbeat and for a classic JoinGroup to a consumer group (KAFKA-20601). The old coordinator had the same problem since static membership was added in 2.3: its size check only looked at the member id too (GroupCoordinator#acceptJoiningMember in 3.9), so this isn't a regression of the new coordinator.

Impact:
* The classic consumer treats GROUP_MAX_SIZE_REACHED as fatal: AbstractCoordinator raises GroupMaxSizeReachedException, and poll() throws it.
* The member can only rejoin after the session of the old member expires and frees a slot.

*Steps to reproduce*
# Set group.max.size=2.
# Start two classic consumers with group.instance.id instance-1 and instance-2, and wait for the group to be stable.
# Kill the second consumer, then start a new consumer with group.instance.id instance-2 before the old member's session expires.
# The JoinGroup of the new consumer gets GROUP_MAX_SIZE_REACHED, and its poll() throws GroupMaxSizeReachedException.

*Expected:* a JoinGroup whose group.instance.id belongs to a static member of the group is accepted whatever the group size, as in consumer groups: the new member replaces the old one, and the group doesn't grow.

summary: Preserve transaction stability when truncating above the high watermark
body:
When a follower truncates diverging uncommitted records above its high watermark (`AbstractFetcherThread.truncateOnFetchResponse` -> `ReplicaFetcherThread.truncate` -> `Partition.truncateTo` -> `UnifiedLog.truncateTo(targetOffset)` with `targetOffset > highWatermark`), `UnifiedLog` and `ProducerStateManager` lose or fail to refresh transactional stability bounds.

Three failure modes occur on current `trunk`:

1. Premature LSO advance / `READ_COMMITTED` isolation violation:
   Write transactional records at offset 0 (< HW = 1) and a COMMIT or ABORT marker at offset 1 (>= HW = 1, unreplicated), roll a segment/producer snapshot at offset 2, append uncommitted tail records at 2..3, and truncate to offset 3. `ProducerStateManager.truncateAndReload` unconditionally calls `unreplicatedTxns.clear()` and reloads snapshot 2, which does not store `unreplicatedTxns`. Once the next append refreshes `firstUnstableOffsetMetadata`, `lastStableOffset` advances from 0 to 1 (= HW) even though the control marker at offset 1 is still unreplicated.

2. LSO regression onto an already-replicated transaction (without a segment roll):
   With completed transaction (0, 1) already replicated (`HW = 2`, `LSO = 2`) and tail records at 2..3, calling `truncateTo(3)` without a snapshot at offset 2 replays `[0, 3)` and re-adds (0, 1) to `unreplicatedTxns`. Because `UnifiedLog.truncateTo` skips `producerStateManager.onHighWatermarkUpdated(highWatermark())` when `highWatermark < logEndOffset`, the next append regresses `lastStableOffset` from 2 back to 0.

3. Stale `firstUnstableOffset` past `logEndOffset`:
   Truncating an ongoing transaction above the high watermark leaves the cached `firstUnstableOffsetMetadata` pointing at the truncated offset because `UnifiedLog.truncateTo` does not call `maybeIncrementFirstUnstableOffset()` on the `highWatermark < logEndOffset` branch.

Affected reads and metrics:
- `FetchIsolation.TXN_COMMITTED` reads (`UnifiedLog.read`, including KIP-392 follower fetches and leader reads if promoted before the high watermark passes the control marker) can return undecided/unreplicated transactional batches or stall behind a regressed LSO.
- `ListOffsets` requests with `IsolationLevel.READ_COMMITTED` (`Partition.fetchOffsetForTimestamp` / LSO lookup).
- `LastStableOffsetLag` metrics.

Relation to existing issues:
- KAFKA-14497 (unreplicated transactions lost on log reopen) shares the snapshot-format limitation, because producer snapshots do not persist `unreplicatedTxns`. Fixing live truncation in memory does not fix log reopen (a fresh `ProducerStateManager` has no in-memory entries to retain), so KAFKA-14497 requires a separate change.
- KAFKA-21551 (`rebuildProducerState` skipping log replay when producer state was empty before truncation) is a separate path and remains out of scope.

summary: Kafka Streams IQv2 KeyQuery returns an uncommitted value on a cache hit with READ_COMMITTED isolation
body:
h3. *Scenario*
 # Enable caching for a RocksDB-backed key-value store in a Kafka Streams application with enable.transactional.statestores=true.
 # Write 10 to key K and commit.
 # Write 20 to the same key. Before the next commit, query K using an IQv2 KeyQuery with READ_COMMITTED isolation and the default unbounded PositionBound.

h3. *Problem*

The query should return 10, the last committed value. On a cache hit, however, CachingKeyValueStore returns 20 without checking the requested isolation level.

The same behavior occurs after flushCache() if the entry remains in the cache. At that point, 20 has reached the RocksDB transaction buffer and is still pending commit. The underlying store returns 10 for the same READ_COMMITTED query.

The State Store Caching section of KIP-892 states that "{*}IQ READ_COMMITTED reads ignore the record cache{*}." The KIP specifies the cache-bypass behavior without prescribing a particular method call. In CachingKeyValueStore, wrapped() provides access to the underlying store
comments: Is this related, or maybe even the same as https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21505 ?

[~mjsax] 

Thanks for taking the time to look into this!

Both issues can expose an uncommitted value to a READ_COMMITTED read. In KAFKA-21505, the format-converting adapter doesn’t forward readOnly(READ_COMMITTED) to the underlying store. In this issue, an IQv2 KeyQuery can return the cached value before it reaches the underlying store, even when there’s no format-converting adapter. Given that difference, it seems reasonable to keep the tickets separate and link them as related...!

What do you think?

summary: Drop the dead code in ListOffsetsRequest
Broker never responds to Produce request with null records, stalling the connection (regression in 3.8.0)
body:
*Reproduction repository:* [https://github.com/akahn/kafka-null-records-repro]

h2. Summary

The {{records}} field of {{PartitionProduceData}} in the Produce request schema is nullable. When a client sends a Produce request in which a partition has {{records=null}}, brokers 3.8.0 and later throw a {{NullPointerException}} and *never send a response*. The broker handles one request at a time per connection, so every later request on the same connection also stays unanswered. The connection stalls until the client's request timeout.

Brokers 3.7.x return {{UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR}} for the partition and the connection stays usable.

Real clients send this. For example, franz-go sends {{records=null}} for a partition whose batch failed after the request was built ([twmb/franz-go#1599|https://github.com/twmb/franz-go/issues/1599]).

h2. Affected versions

Tested with {{apache/kafka}} images, single-node KRaft, with the highest Produce version each broker supports (v10 to v13). Produce v3 and v9 against 4.4.0 give the same result.

||Version||Result||
|3.7.0, 3.7.2|Partition error {{UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR}}, connection usable|
|3.8.0, 3.9.0, 4.0.0, 4.1.0, 4.2.0, 4.3.0, 4.4.0|*No response, connection stalled*|

h2. Reproduce

Requires Docker.

{noformat}
git clone https://github.com/akahn/kafka-null-records-repro
cd kafka-null-records-repro
./repro.sh 3.7.2 3.8.0     # default; pass any apache/kafka tags (3.7.0+)
{noformat}

For each version, {{repro.sh}} starts a fresh broker ({{docker-compose.yml}}, {{KAFKA_VERSION}} selects the image tag), creates a topic, and runs {{main.go}}. {{main.go}} uses a raw TCP connection and uses franz-go's {{kmsg}} package only to encode and decode messages. On one connection it sends:

# {{ApiVersions}} and {{Metadata}}.
# Control: {{Produce}} with a valid one-record batch, {{acks=1}}. The broker answers.
# {{Produce}} with partition 0 {{records=null}}, then {{ApiVersions}} (pipelined).

The exit code is 1 if the broker does not answer step 3 within 10 seconds.

You can also run the client against an existing broker: {{go run . -broker host:9092 -topic <topic>}}.

h3. 3.7.2 output

{noformat}
-> Produce v10 partition 0: records=null
-> ApiVersions v0
<- Produce v10 partition 0: error=UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR: The server experienced an unexpected error when processing the request.
<- ApiVersions v0 error=NONE

RESULT: NOT AFFECTED. The broker answered the records=null Produce request.
{noformat}

h3. 3.8.0 output

{noformat}
-> Produce v10 partition 0: records=null
-> ApiVersions v0
<- Produce v10: NO RESPONSE after 10s

RESULT: AFFECTED. The broker did not answer the records=null Produce request, and the connection is stalled.
{noformat}

Broker log (3.8.0):

{noformat}
ERROR [Kafka Request Handler 3 on Broker 1], Exception when handling request (kafka.server.KafkaRequestHandler)
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "org.apache.kafka.common.record.BaseRecords.sizeInBytes()" because the return value of "org.apache.kafka.

summary: suppress() for windowed-Serdes does not work with default serdes
body:
The suppress() operator either inherits serdes from its upstream operator or falls back to default serdes from the config.

If the upstream operator is an windowed aggregation, the window-aggregation operator wraps the user passed-in serde with a window-serde and pushed it into suppress() – however, if default serdes are used, the window-aggregation operator cannot push anything into suppress(). At runtime, it just creates a default serde and wraps it according. For this case, suppress() also falls back to default serdes; however, it does not wrap the serde and thus a ClassCastException is thrown when the serde is used later.

suppress() is already aware if the upstream aggregation is time/session windowed or not and thus should use this information to wrap default serdes accordingly.

The current workaround for windowed-suppress is to overwrite the default serde upstream to suppress(), such that suppress() inherits serdes and does not fall back to default serdes.

 

For the search engines, when using Avro, this results in a ClassCastException:

{{Caused by: java.lang.ClassCastException: class org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.Windowed cannot be cast to class org.apache.avro.specific.SpecificRecord (org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.Windowed and org.apache.avro.specific.SpecificRecord are in unnamed module of loader 'app') at io.confluent.kafka.streams.serdes.avro.SpecificAvroSerializer.serialize(SpecificAvroSerializer.java:38)}}
comments:
Thanks for the report, [~mjsax]!

Just a quick additional note for whoever picks this up: To properly parameterize windowed serdes, you need extra information about the windows (eg the window size). Theoretically, the suppress operator could find this out by traversing the topology upstream to find it on its window-definition ancestor, but it might get a bit brittle. If this turns out to be a mess, it would probably be cleaner just to implement https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-9260 instead, which would also fix this issue.
Can I work on this issue?

summary: Add sugar method "join" to KafkaFuture
body:
KafkaFuture is one of the oldest and most commonly used classes in our public APIs. We introduced the method {{toCompletionStage}} to reduce the gap from the modern async style. It works, but it could be better. We assumed users would use {{toCompletionStage}} to chain the pipeline, but we missed the users who prefer the blocking style in lambdas. Unfortunately, the blocking method {{get}} has checked exceptions in its signature.

In short, this ticket introduces {{join}} to KafkaFuture. It could be a simple method with a default implementation, such as {{{}toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().join(){}}}.

summary: Classic to consumer group conversion can assign a partition to two members
body:
When a classic group is converted to a consumer group during a rebalance that started in CompletingRebalance, the converted members own no partitions, even though cooperative members still consume theirs. The first target assignment of the consumer group then gives those partitions to other members, so two members consume the same partitions until the old owners rejoin and revoke them.

A rebalance starts in CompletingRebalance, for example, when a member joins or leaves before the leader sends its SyncGroup, or when the write of the leader's assignment fails. The group coordinator then sets the in-memory assignment of every member to empty, and it stays empty until the next SyncGroup of the leader, even across the next join phase. The reset is never written to the log, and cooperative members keep their partitions meanwhile. {{ConsumerGroup.fromClassicGroup}} builds the assigned partitions and the target assignment of each member from these empty assignments.

Steps to reproduce, with group.consumer.migration.policy=upgrade or bidirectional:
# Two classic consumers using cooperative-sticky own partitions of a topic at generation 1.
# A third classic consumer joins. The join phase completes, and the group waits in CompletingRebalance for the SyncGroup of the leader.
# A fourth classic consumer joins before that SyncGroup, which starts a new rebalance.
# Before the leader's next SyncGroup, a consumer with group.protocol=consumer joins the group, which converts it to a consumer group.
# The new consumer, or another member, is assigned partitions that the first two consumers still consume.

Impact:
* For a short window, two consumers process the same partitions. The window ends when the old owners rejoin at their next poll() and revoke the partitions, so it lasts up to one poll loop, bounded by max.poll.interval.ms.
* At-least-once applications process records twice. When the old owners revoke the partitions, their commits in onPartitionsRevoked are accepted and can overwrite the offsets of the new owners.
* Exactly-once applications lose the guarantee during the window, because the old owners are not fenced.
* Only cooperative members are affected. Eager members give up their partitions before they rejoin.

summary: ConsumerGroupHeartbeat returns member epoch 0 after upgrading a generation-0 classic group when the assignor is offloaded
body:
When a classic group is upgraded to a consumer group before completing its first rebalance, the upgraded group's target assignment epoch is 0, because the members hold no assignment yet. When the assignor is offloaded, the ConsumerGroupHeartbeat that triggers the upgrade schedules a new target assignment and replies using the current target assignment. The member is reconciled to target assignment epoch 0, and the response returns member epoch 0. Epoch 0 is reserved for members joining a group, so the coordinator must never return it.

This happens for every upgrade at generation 0, whether the upgrade is triggered by a new member or by static member replacement. Without offload, only static member replacement is affected (KAFKA-21581), because a new member's join computes the new target assignment synchronously.

KAFKA-21581 and KAFKA-21582 do not cover this. Their fix bumps the group epoch when a rebalancing classic group is upgraded, so that a new target assignment is computed. Without offload, the new target assignment is computed in the same heartbeat, and the member is reconciled to it at epoch 1. With offload, the new target assignment is computed later, and until it is installed the member can only be reconciled to the existing target assignment. At generation 0, that target assignment has epoch 0.

*Steps to reproduce*
# Set {{group.consumer.migration.policy}} to {{upgrade}} and {{group.consumer.assignor.offload.enable}} to {{true}}. Set {{group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms}} high enough that the classic group's initial rebalance doesn't complete during the test.
# A classic member joins a new group G. The group goes to PreparingRebalance at generation 0, and the JoinGroup stays pending.
# Before the initial rebalance completes, a consumer-protocol member sends ConsumerGroupHeartbeat to G with member epoch 0.
# The coordinator upgrades G to a consumer group with target assignment epoch 0. The heartbeat bumps the group epoch and offloads the new target assignment.
# The heartbeat replies with the current target assignment, at epoch 0.
# The response returns member epoch 0.

*Expected:* the member gets an epoch greater than 0. New consumer groups avoid this by starting at target assignment epoch 1 with an empty assignment (KAFKA-20268). An upgraded generation-0 group should start the same way.

summary: AcknowledgeType.RENEW re-delivers records to application via poll() in explicit acknowledgement mode, undocumented and inconsistent with broker-side contract
body:
AcknowledgeType.RENEW is documented as a way to extend the acquisition lock on a record that is still being processed, without changing the record's state on the broker. However, the client-side implementation silently re-delivers the same records back to the application on the next poll() call. This behavior is nowhere documented, violates the explicit acknowledgement mode invariant, and diverges from the broker-side contract.

RENEW simultaneously satisfies two contradictory contracts:

Context ----What RENEW implies
ensureInFlightAcknowledgedIfExplicitAcknowledgement() --- Record IS acknowledged — gate passes
collect() / takeRenewedRecords() ----Record is NOT done — re-delivered on next poll()


Two acceptable resolutions, depending on intended design:
Option A — RENEW means "extend lock only, no re-delivery":

Option B — RENEW means "extend lock and re-deliver to same consumer" (current behavior, make it explicit).

Our usecase : 

We are building an async pipeline where records are consumed, published to a downstream system asynchronously, and then acknowledged. We need to:

 1.  Hold the broker acquisition lock while async publish is in flight.
 2.  Not lose the record if publish takes longer than one poll cycle.
 3.  Call ACCEPT once publish confirms, RELEASE if it fails.
comments: The javadoc for `KafkaShareConsumer` explains the behaviour for renew acknowledgements. It's Option B above.

I believe it is better to extend the lock, until consumer alive or till the next poll or till the next renew/accept acknowledged sent from consumer for the record?

summary: PR tools should not rewrite the PR description written by the author
body:
The PR description becomes the commit message when a PR is merged. Two scripts edit it automatically:
 * {{.github/scripts/pr-format.py}} (PR Linter) re-wraps the whole description to 72 characters and writes it back.
 * {{.github/scripts/pr-reviewers-trailer.py}} adds reviewers to the {{Reviewers:}} trailer.

We want four things at the same time:
 * The author's text stays as the author wrote it.
 * Commit messages are tidy, with lines of at most 72 characters.
 * Reviewer credit is reliable. For this, {{Reviewers:}} must be a valid git trailer.
 * Committers do not have to type the reviewers by hand.

Today the tools give up the first one to get the second one. To re-wrap the text, {{pr-format.py}} has to guess its structure. When the guess is wrong, the description is damaged:
 * Adjacent trailers are joined into one line. This is the case that was first reported here:
{code}
Co-Authored-By: Some Bot <contributor@example.invalid>
Reviewers: Ken Huang <contributor@example.invalid>, Federico Valeri <contributor@example.invalid>{code}
becomes
{code}
Co-Authored-By: Some Bot <contributor@example.invalid> Reviewers: Ken
Huang <contributor@example.invalid>, Federico Valeri <contributor@example.invalid>{code}
{{Reviewers:}} is now part of the {{Co-Authored-By:}} value. The next review adds a second {{Reviewers:}} trailer.
 * The rows of a Markdown table are joined into one paragraph.

Each new case needs one more special rule in the formatter. Lists, code blocks and backticks already have one.

This trade is based on an assumption that is not true today. The re-wrap was added in KAFKA-19013 with this reason: PRs will be merged with the merge queue, GitHub wraps the commit message there, and the committer cannot edit it. So the tool must wrap the text first.

Both parts of that reason do not hold:
 * The merge queue is not in use on {{apache/kafka}}. The rulesets have no {{merge_queue}} rule, the GraphQL field {{mergeQueue(branch: "trunk")}} is null, and no workflow has a {{merge_group}} trigger.
 * In tests on a fork, GitHub wraps long lines and converts CRLF to LF by itself when it builds the default squash commit message from the PR description. This was checked with the API and in the merge dialog of the web page. It does not join short lines and it does not change code blocks.

So we can keep the author's text and still get tidy commit messages. One gap is left. GitHub does not indent the lines that it wraps, and a wrapped {{Reviewers:}} trailer without indentation is cut short. So a long {{Reviewers:}} trailer is the only text that a tool still has to fold.

Proposed change:
 # {{pr-format.py}} only reads the PR. It checks the title and the description and reports the result. It never edits the description.
 # {{pr-reviewers-trailer.py}} is the only script that edits the description. It changes only the {{Reviewers:}} trailer in the last paragraph and keeps all other text byte for byte.
 # {{pr-reviewers-trailer.py}} folds a {{Reviewers:}} trail

summary: Upgrading a classic group during a rebalance does not trigger a new target assignment when the upgrading member does not bump the group epoch
body:
{{ConsumerGroup#fromClassicGroup}} sets the group epoch and the target assignment epoch to the classic group's generation, and it takes the previous generation's assignments as the target assignment. When the classic group is in PreparingRebalance or CompletingRebalance, it is waiting for a new assignment, so these values are stale. The upgrade is supposed to get a fresh assignment from the epoch bump caused by the joining member. When the member that triggers the upgrade does not bump the epoch, the coordinator treats the stale target assignment as up to date. Two such members are:
 * A consumer-protocol static member that replaces a classic static member with the same subscription.
 * A new consumer-protocol member that subscribes with a regex that resolves to no topics. A new regex does not bump the group epoch until it is resolved, and resolving it to no topics does not bump it either.

*Steps to reproduce (static member replacement)*
 # Set {{group.consumer.migration.policy}} to {{{}upgrade{}}}, and set {{group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms}} high enough that the classic group's initial rebalance doesn't complete during the test.
 # A classic static member with {{group.instance.id}} X joins a new group G. The group goes to PreparingRebalance at generation 0 and the JoinGroup stays pending.
 # Before the initial rebalance completes, a consumer-protocol member with a new member id sends ConsumerGroupHeartbeat to G with member epoch 0, {{instanceId}} X, and the same subscription as the classic member.
 # The coordinator upgrades G to a consumer group at group epoch 0 and target assignment epoch 0. The consumer member replaces the classic static member and is reset to epoch 0.
 # The subscription is unchanged, so the group epoch isn't bumped. The coordinator considers the target assignment at epoch 0 up to date, and reconciles the new member to it.
 # The heartbeat response returns member epoch 0.

*Steps to reproduce (regex that resolves to no topics)*
 # Set {{group.consumer.migration.policy}} to {{{}upgrade{}}}, and set {{group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms}} high enough that the classic group's initial rebalance doesn't complete during the test.
 # A classic member joins a new group G. The group goes to PreparingRebalance at generation 0 and the JoinGroup stays pending.
 # Before the initial rebalance completes, a consumer-protocol member with a new member id sends ConsumerGroupHeartbeat to G with member epoch 0 and a {{subscribedTopicRegex}} that matches no topic.
 # The coordinator upgrades G to a consumer group at group epoch 0 and target assignment epoch 0. The new member's regex is not resolved yet, so its join doesn't bump the group epoch.
 # The coordinator considers the target assignment at epoch 0 up to date, and reconciles the new member to it. The heartbeat response returns member epoch 0.

summary: JoinGroup with a known member id removes an empty consumer or streams group in memory only
body:
When a classic consumer sends a JoinGroup with a member id to a consumer group or a streams group that has no members, the group coordinator deletes the group in memory and adds its tombstones to the records of the request. The request is then rejected with UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID because the member id is unknown, and the records are dropped. The group is gone from memory, but its deletion is never written to the log.

A classic consumer sends such a request, for example, when it was removed from the group after its session timed out, it was the last member, and it rejoins with its previous member id.

Impact:
* Once the next write to the same __consumer_offsets partition is committed, the group disappears from ConsumerGroupDescribe, StreamsGroupDescribe, DescribeGroups and ListGroups, which read at the last committed offset, while the log still holds it.
* The group comes back when the partition is loaded again, for example after a coordinator failover.
* The next JoinGroup with an unknown member id creates a classic group in its place without writing the tombstones of the consumer or streams group, so the log keeps records of a group that no longer exists.

summary: Data loss: tiered size-retention deletes in-retention data from both tiers after leader election when highestOffsetInRemoteStorage is unset (-1)
body:
Size-based remote retention deletes the oldest data when {{{}onlyLocalLogSegmentsSize + remoteLogSizeBytes > retention.bytes{}}}. {{onlyLocalLogSegmentsSize}} sums segments with {{{}baseOffset >= highestOffsetInRemoteStorage(){}}}. That field is in-memory, initialised to {{{}-1{}}}, not recovered on startup, and seeded only by the copy and follower tasks.

After a leader election the copy and expiration tasks both start at {{-1}} and are scheduled with {{initialDelay = 0}} on separate thread pools, so they race. If the expiration task runs first, the filter {{baseOffset >= -1}} matches the entire local log, and those segments are also counted in {{remoteLogSizeBytes}} — the same offsets counted twice. The apparent size roughly doubles, {{retention.bytes}} appears breached, and the broker deletes the oldest remote segments and advances {{{}logStartOffset{}}}. {{logStartOffset}} replicates to followers, so each replica deletes local segments below the new floor. In-retention data is removed from both tiers on all replicas; consumers receive {{OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE}} for the removed offsets.

The follower path already seeds this offset before it can cause harm: {{RLMFollowerTask.execute()}} does so with the comment _"so that the local log segments are not deleted before they are copied to remote storage."_ The leader/expiration path, which runs size-retention, has no equivalent step.
h2. Example - one affected partition

A 24-partition test topic at its cap ({{{}retention.bytes = 134217728{}}} = 128 MiB, {{{}local.retention.bytes = -2{}}}, {{{}retention.ms = -1{}}}); both tiers held the full window (remote ≈ local ≈ cap, copy-lag 0). One broker is restarted and becomes the fresh leader of partition {{{}...-1{}}}; ~40 s later its expiration task runs while {{highestOffsetInRemoteStorage}} is still {{{}-1{}}}:
{code:java}
# leader shared-sasl-kafka-1 — size-retention on a partition whose unique data is ~128 MiB:
08:43:59.420  RLMExpirationTask ...repro.v1-1] About to delete remote log segment ... due to
              retention size 134217728 breach. Log size after deletion will be 282854919
              #   cap = 134217728 (128 MiB); computed ~270 MiB = local(~128) + remote(~128), counted twice
              #   ... deletes 9 remote segments, recomputing downward until just above the cap:
08:43:59.430  ... due to retention size 134217728 breach. Log size after deletion will be 149820412
08:43:59.430  UnifiedLog ...repro.v1-1] Incremented log start offset to 289616 due to segment deletion

# the new log-start floor replicates to the followers:
08:43:59.680  shared-sasl-kafka-0 ...repro.v1-1] Incremented log start offset to 289616 due to leader offset increment
08:44:36.319  shared-sasl-kafka-2 ...repro.v1-1] Incremented log start offset to 289616 due to leader offset increment

# each replica then deletes its local segments below the floor — data now gone from BOTH tiers:
08:44:21.146  UnifiedLog ...repro.v1-1] Deleting segments due to local log start o

summary: Improve refiner performance
body:
We landed the first version of the refiner w/o any JMH results. If we need to optimize for better performance a few ideas to explore (some already discussed during code review):
 * replace Java Streams API usage with “native” loops

 * replace list+sort with heap

 * cache more helper data structures (cf below)

 * maybe integrate deeper with reconciler

About helper data structures: currently, the GC uses an in-memory cache to store the intermediate assignment. We could extent this, to also store helper data structures like “load index” which change incrementally for most cases, and we should be able to re-used across refiner runs (atm, the refiner computes all helpers from scratch on each run). Other candidates for caching is “funding candidate order” (ie, in which order we plan to assign warmup tasks — it’s mainly load based so keeping it across refiner runs and maintaining it incrementally might also cut costs; for this case, a heap might become really beneficial).

summary: LoginManager release can block unbounded while holding the class lock affecting other clients
body:
LoginManager.release holds the JVM-wide class lock while it closes the {{Login}} ([LoginManager.java#L155-L164|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/30a33d5a8bc8c8d6d41516b9e7113dc822b867be/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/authenticator/LoginManager.java#L155-L164]). For OAUTHBEARER, ExpiringCredentialRefreshingLogin.close interrupts the refresh thread once, then calls {{join()}} with no timeout ([ExpiringCredentialRefreshingLogin.java#L248-L259|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/30a33d5a8bc8c8d6d41516b9e7113dc822b867be/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/oauthbearer/internals/expiring/ExpiringCredentialRefreshingLogin.java#L248-L259]).

The refresh thread exits only if it sees its interrupt flag after one of its own sleeps ([L94-L95|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/30a33d5a8bc8c8d6d41516b9e7113dc822b867be/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/oauthbearer/internals/expiring/ExpiringCredentialRefreshingLogin.java#L94-L95], [L119-L120|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/30a33d5a8bc8c8d6d41516b9e7113dc822b867be/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/oauthbearer/internals/expiring/ExpiringCredentialRefreshingLogin.java#L119-L120]). If the interrupt arrives during a re-login and the configured {{sasl.login.callback.handler.class}} clears the flag, the thread keeps refreshing forever. For example, the handler might catch the {{InterruptedException}} from a blocking HTTP call and rethrow it wrapped. Then {{join()}} never returns, and {{LoginManager.class}} stays held.

This would let the client hanging in {{{}close(){}}}. Because {{acquireLoginManager()}} and {{release()}} both take the same lock ([L109|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/30a33d5a8bc8c8d6d41516b9e7113dc822b867be/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/authenticator/LoginManager.java#L109], [L155|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/30a33d5a8bc8c8d6d41516b9e7113dc822b867be/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/authenticator/LoginManager.java#L155]), creating or closing any other SASL client in the JVM blocks too.

summary: Streams EOS: healthy tasks' outputs are aborted during corruption handling while their input progress is kept
body:
Under exactly_once_v2 with the classic group protocol, TaskManager#handleCorruption commits the non-corrupted RUNNING tasks before closing the corrupted active tasks dirty. It does this because the dirty close aborts the thread's ongoing transaction.

If a rebalance is in progress, commitTasksAndMaybeUpdateCommittableOffsets returns -1 without committing, and handleCorruption ignores the return value. closeDirtyAndRevive then calls RecordCollectorImpl#closeDirty, which calls StreamsProducer#abortTransaction. That aborts the shared transaction, including the uncommitted outputs of the healthy tasks.

Only the closed tasks get input offset resets. The healthy tasks stay RUNNING with their consumed offsets and commitNeeded intact. A later commit, for example in handleRevocation, commits those input offsets. The outputs of the records processed between the last successful commit and the abort are lost.

summary: Headers-aware store adapters don't propagate readOnly(IsolationLevel), so READ_COMMITTED reads see uncommitted writes
body:
When a headers-aware store is built on top of a store in the old (non-headers) format, the builder inserts a format-converting adapter between the outer layers and the inner store:

- PlainToHeadersStoreAdapter, TimestampedToHeadersStoreAdapter (TimestampedKeyValueStoreBuilderWithHeaders)
- PlainToHeadersWindowStoreAdapter, TimestampedToHeadersWindowStoreAdapter (TimestampedWindowStoreWithHeadersBuilder)
- SessionToHeadersStoreAdapter (SessionStoreWithHeadersBuilder)

None of these adapters override readOnly(IsolationLevel), so they inherit the interface default, which returns `this`.

With enable.transactional.statestores=true, the outer layers (metered, change-logging, caching) pass readOnly(level) down to their inner store, and the RocksDB stores (RocksDBStore, RocksDBWindowStore, RocksDBSessionStore) override it so that READ_COMMITTED skips the transaction buffer. The chain stops at the adapter: it returns itself, and reads keep going through the inner store's transaction buffer. A READ_COMMITTED read therefore sees writes that have not been committed yet.

Cause: the adapters (KAFKA-20134, KAFKA-20158) were added before readOnly(IsolationLevel) was introduced for these store types (KAFKA-20496, KAFKA-20768), and they were not updated when it was.

Affected only when all of these hold:
- enable.transactional.statestores=true
- a headers-aware store is backed by a store in the old format (adapter path)
- the store is read with READ_COMMITTED

Proposed fix: override readOnly(IsolationLevel) in each adapter to call inner.readOnly(level) and wrap the result in the same format conversion the adapter applies to normal reads. Then remove readOnly from SPECIAL in TimestampedToHeadersWindowStoreAdapterCompletenessTest and SessionToHeadersStoreAdapterCompletenessTest (added in KAFKA-20328, https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22992), and add a test that a READ_COMMITTED view through each adapter does not see staged writes.

Related: the older timestamped adapters (KeyValueToTimestampedKeyValueByteStoreAdapter, WindowToTimestampedWindowByteStoreAdapter) do not override readOnly either and may have the same gap.
comments:
Hi, I'd like to work on this issue. I've posted a PR that propagates {{readOnly(IsolationLevel)}} through all seven format-converting adapters (the five headers-aware ones named in the description, plus the two older timestamped adapters mentioned under "Related"):

https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/24253

Each adapter now delegates to the inner store's read-only view and applies its format conversion on top, so a READ_COMMITTED read through an adapter no longer goes through the inner store's transaction buffer and cannot see uncommitted writes. Tests cover each adapter.

One note: the CompletenessTest SPECIAL cleanups suggested in the description are not included, since KAFKA-20328 (PR #22992) is not merged into trunk yet — those tests don't exist on trunk today.

Happy to adjust if reviewers prefer a different direction.

summary: Java client does not honor GetTelemetrySubscriptionsResponse.TelemetryMaxBytes
body:
KIP-714 says a client that receives TELEMETRY_TOO_LARGE must "Reduce the size of the metrics payload so its size does not exceed GetTelemetrySubscriptionsResponse.TelemetryMaxBytes." The broker sends the value in every subscription response ({{{}ClientMetricsManager{}}} line 383, {{{}setTelemetryMaxBytes{}}}).

{{ClientTelemetryReporter}} never reads it. {{createPushRequest}} collects, serializes, compresses, and sends the payload with no size check, and {{ClientTelemetrySubscription}} does not store the value. On TELEMETRY_TOO_LARGE the client only reschedules a similarly-sized payload ({{{}maybeFetchErrorIntervalMs{}}}), so it repeats a push the broker will reject with {{TELEMETRY_TOO_LARGE}} every interval.

Suggested fix: keep {{telemetryMaxBytes}} in {{{}ClientTelemetrySubscription{}}}, compare the compressed payload against it before sending, and when the payload is too large either log a warning with the size and the metric count and skip the push, or drop lower-priority metric groups until it fits.

summary: Async consumer can apply a HB response from before a poll timer expiration leave + rejoin
body:
When the poll timer expires the async consumer sends a leave HB (even if there was one in-flight) and clears the in-flight flag. The earlier HB response will still be received (AbstractMembershipManager#onHeartbeatSuccess), and that logic already considers it has to drop responses that are not relevant anymore, which is if the member is LEAVING, not in the group etc.

But if the situation above combines with the app calling poll again before that response arrives, the member is already JOINING, so the old response would be accepted.

This is probably hard to trigger in real life scenarios: needs poll timer expiration while a heartbeat is in flight + the application to call poll before the response to the first in-flight arrives, and (not sure but) I guess it needs the response to include an assignment change for this to be harmful, otherwise the impact it's just unneeded processing on the consumer. But if it has assignment change it could end up reconciliing and triggering callbacks for the old assignment when the member is already rejoining.

We should fix to not apply HB responses for requests sent before the leave, even if the member is not LEAVING (may be joining). Let's also look at how the in-flight flag is cleared in this case. And this probably needs fixing consistently for the consumer and streams membership managers.

summary: Potential data loss during KRaft migration due to a lost ZooKeeper acknowledgement on /migration write
body:
A lost ZooKeeper acknowledgment on a successful {{/migration}} znode write can cause the KRaft migration driver to mistake its own prior write for a conflicting one, permanently stalling it once it reaches the {{DUAL_WRITE}} stage. This prevents further writes to ZooKeeper, allowing the state in between KRaft and ZooKeeper to diverge during the migration.

This happens because the client the migration uses to talk to ZooKeeper will retry an identical request to {{/migration}} if it sees a connection loss. If the original request had actually already succeeded on the server, but only its acknowledgment was lost, the retry sends the same expected version of the {{/migration}} znode again. Since that version has already moved on, ZooKeeper rejects the retry as a version conflict, even though nothing is actually wrong.

The migration driver currently has no way to tell this apart from a genuine conflict caused by a second controller writing at the same time, so it treats every such rejection as a hard failure. Because the write is treated as a failure, the driver's own record of what version the {{/migration}} znode is currently at never gets corrected, and stays at the old, stale value. Every subsequent write then reuses that same stale value and hits the same rejection, indefinitely. The driver becomes permanently stuck, unable to make further migration progress, until an unrelated event, such as a new controller election, forces an unconditional resynchronization of {{{}/migration{}}}.

While stuck, ZooKeeper stops receiving updates from the controller, and any ZK-mode brokers that rely on ZooKeeper for their view of cluster state are never notified of the corresponding changes via RPCs either. This causes the states in ZooKeeper and KRaft to diverge, which can destabilize the cluster further.

This is of particular concern when some, but not all, brokers have already been restarted into their KRaft mode. The remaining ZK-mode brokers are left running on an increasingly outdated view of the cluster state. In the worst case, this can cause real data loss if the KRaft side elects a new partition leader while the driver is stuck. As that change is never propagated to ZooKeeper, and the ZK-mode brokers are never notified of it via RPC either, the old leader can continue to operate under the stale, lower epoch. The old leader can keep accepting and acknowledging produce requests it is no longer authorized to serve. When it eventually discovers the true, higher-epoch leader, it must truncate its own log to reconcile, silently discarding any writes it had already acknowledged to producers in the meantime.

[{{KafkaZkClient}} |https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/3.9.2/core/src/main/scala/kafka/zk/KafkaZkClient.scala]exposes two methods used to write to the {{/migration}} znode in ZooKeeper during a ZK-to-KRaft migration:
 # the standalone [{{updateMigrationState}}|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/5e9866f43ab8e7e41ef39e5584ac5001938132
comments: [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23639]

summary: KRaft migration rollback causes offline partitions when KRaft epoch exceeds ZK controller epoch
body:
When reverting to ZooKeeper mode during a KRaft migration, partitions that experienced state changes (ISR changes, leader elections, etc.) during the dual-write phase may be left without a leader after the rollback and go offline.

This occurs because during the dual-write phase, the KRaft controller epoch (a separate counter from the ZooKeeper controller epoch), is written into each affected partition's state znode as the {{controller_epoch}} field.

On rollback, a ZooKeeper broker wins the controller election and increments the {{/controller_epoch}} znode by 1 to derive its own epoch. When it then attempts to elect leaders for partitions, it reads back each partition state znode and checks whether the stored {{controller_epoch}} exceeds its own. If the KRaft controller epoch written during the dual-write phase was higher than this newly derived ZooKeeper epoch, the controller treats the znode as having been written by a newer controller, aborts the leader election for that partition, and the partition goes offline.
h3. Example:

During the migration, our KRaft controllers had an epoch of 502 . This can be seen in the {{/migration}} znode:
{code:java}
get /migration
{"version":0,"kraft_metadata_offset":870200,"kraft_controller_id":902,"kraft_metadata_epoch":502,"kraft_controller_epoch":502}
{code}
This epoch was written as the {{controller_epoch}} value in the partition state znode for several partitions, e.g.:
{code:java}
get /brokers/topics/__consumer_offsets/partitions/45/state
{"controller_epoch":502,"leader":2,"version":1,"leader_epoch":56,"isr":[0,1,2]} {code}
Despite this, the value in the {{/controller_epoch}} znode remains much lower, as it’s its own counter:
{code:java}
get /controller_epoch
226
{code}
Leading to these errors when the ZK broker was elected as the controller on rollback with this lower epoch:
{code:java}
message:  [Controller id=0 epoch=226] Controller 0 epoch 226 failed to change state for partition __consumer_offsets-45 from OfflinePartition to OnlinePartition
throwable: { [-]
      class:  kafka.common.StateChangeFailedException
      msg:  Aborted leader election for partition __consumer_offsets-45 since the LeaderAndIsr path was already written by another controller. This probably means that the current controller 0 went through a soft failure and another controller was elected with epoch 502.
      stack: [ [-]
        kafka.controller.ZkPartitionStateMachine.$anonfun$doElectLeaderForPartitions$2(PartitionStateMachine.scala:389)
        scala.collection.IterableOnceOps.foreach(IterableOnce.scala:576)
        scala.collection.IterableOnceOps.foreach$(IterableOnce.scala:574)
        scala.collection.AbstractIterable.foreach(Iterable.scala:933)
        kafka.controller.ZkPartitionStateMachine.doElectLeaderForPartitions(PartitionStateMachine.scala:379)
        kafka.controller.ZkPartitionStateMachine.electLeaderForPartitions(PartitionStateMachine.scala:336)
        kafka.controller.ZkPartitionStateMachine.doHandleStat

summary: Streams group coordinator undercounts repartition topic partitions when it visits a downstream subtopology before its upstream dependency
body:
*Description*

A Kafka Streams application using {{group.protocol=streams}} reads from two input topics, {{high}} with 3 partitions and {{low}} with 1 partition. It repartitions {{{}high{}}}, merges the result with {{{}low{}}}, and repartitions the merged stream. Both {{repartition()}} calls leave the partition count unspecified.

 
{code:java}
KStream<String, String> low = builder.stream("low");
KStream<String, String> upstream = builder.<String, String>stream("high")
    .repartition(Repartitioned.as("upstream"));

low.merge(upstream)
    .repartition(Repartitioned.as("downstream"))
    .to("output");
{code}
 

The expected partition count for {{upstream}} is 3 because its only input is {{{}high{}}}. The expected count for {{downstream}} is also 3, the maximum of its two inputs. However, the group coordinator requests {*}3 partitions for {{upstream}} and only 1 for {{downstream}}{*}.

*Both classic protocol and streams protocol have same problem.*

 

*Cause and impact*

With {{low}} registered first in this topology, the subtopology that writes to {{downstream}} gets ID {{{}0{}}}, and the one that writes to {{upstream}} gets ID {{{}1{}}}. When the coordinator visits subtopology {{0}} first, it knows that {{low}} has 1 partition but has yet to determine the partition count for {{{}upstream{}}}.

The coordinator skips the unresolved input and records {{{}downstream=1{}}}. When it later determines that {{{}upstream=3{}}}, it does not revisit {{downstream}} because that topic already has a recorded count. As a result, the coordinator can request a new {{downstream}} topic with only 1 partition. If the topic already exists with the expected 3 partitions, the coordinator can reject it with {{{}expected 1, found 3{}}}.

 

*Subsequent member joins and coordinator failover*

The partition count is determined at the group level. Once the group has a {{{}ConfiguredTopology{}}}, the coordinator reuses it when another member joins with a matching topology and the relevant topic metadata is unchanged. A subsequent join therefore does not change {{downstream}} from 1 to 3.

On failover, the new coordinator loses the in-memory {{ConfiguredTopology}} but restores the group topology from {{{}__consumer_offsets{}}}. If the first member to join after failover supplies a matching topology, the coordinator recalculates the partition count from the restored group topology. With the same calculation logic and topic metadata, this example resolves to {{downstream=1}} again. If the topic has yet to be created, the coordinator requests 1 partition. If it already exists with 1 partition, the coordinator accepts it.

 

*How to reproduce*
{code:java}
// Start broker and execute this commands in your terminal
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic high   --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1     11:34:37
$ bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic low    --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
$ bin/kafka-topics
comments:
Thanks for the detailed report, [~chickenchickenlove]. I reproduced this on both paths.

The cause is in the partition count calculation for repartition topics. For a topic written by a subtopology, it takes the maximum over the inputs that happen to be known when that subtopology is visited, and skips repartition inputs whose count is not decided yet. The count is then fixed and never revisited. So {{downstream}} gets 1 when the subtopology writing it is visited before the one writing {{{}upstream{}}}. Both the classic assignor and the streams group coordinator have this logic. The result depends on visit order: the order of subtopology IDs for the streams protocol, and the iteration order of a {{HashSet}} for classic. That explains the difference you saw when migrating between the two protocols.

The fix itself is small: decide a topic's count only once all its inputs are resolved. The difficulty is compatibility. Existing applications may already have a {{downstream}} topic with 1 partition, and with a plain fix they would fail with {{expected 3, found 1}} on the next rebalance, or on the next coordinator failover for the streams protocol. The topic cannot be repartitioned in place either, because the downstream subtopology is typically stateful.

My proposal is to keep the existing topic in that case. When a repartition topic already exists with a count that an old version could have produced from a subset of its inputs, that count is kept and is also used for repartition topics further downstream. Concretely, it is kept only if all three of these hold:
 * it is smaller than the new maximum,
 * it is at least as large as every external input, because those were always known,
 * it equals the partition count of one of the inputs.

Any other mismatch, for example a user growing an input topic, still fails as before. New topics get the correct maximum. This needs no config or API change, and it also makes behaviour consistent when migrating between protocols and during rolling upgrades.

Does anyone see a case where an existing topic with a smaller count should be rejected?

Do you want to work on this problem? I have a draft PR now

summary: Return INVALID_COMMIT_OFFSET_SIZE from OffsetCommit and TxnOffsetCommit when the offsets exceed the maximum batch size
body:
OffsetCommit and TxnOffsetCommit write one record for each committed partition in one atomic batch. When the batch exceeds max.message.bytes of __consumer_offsets, the old group coordinator returned INVALID_COMMIT_OFFSET_SIZE.

The new group coordinator returns UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR, because CoordinatorOperationExceptionHelper maps MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE and RECORD_LIST_TOO_LARGE to it for every API. 

This has been an issue since AK 4.0.

The fix is to map MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE and RECORD_LIST_TOO_LARGE to INVALID_COMMIT_OFFSET_SIZE in GroupCoordinatorService.commitOffsets and commitTransactionalOffsets. The protocol stays unchanged.

summary: Add MirrorPartitionMetadata record type
body:
KIP-1279 needs an immutable snapshot type to carry per-partition mirror metadata throughout the system. The coordinator persists it, the broker acts on it, and various components read it to make state transition decisions.

Add a MirrorPartitionMetadata record in org.apache.kafka.server.mirror within the server-common module. This class is referenced from multiple modules (core, metadata, mirror-coordinator) and server-common is the lowest common dependency that avoids circular module dependencies.

The record holds the partition's current mirror state, state epoch, last mirrored epoch and offset, error information, retry attempt, and previous state.

summary: An upgrade after a topic was re-created with fewer partitions assigns partitions that don't exist
body:
When a consumer that uses the consumer protocol joins a classic group, the group coordinator converts the classic group to a consumer group. The converted members keep the last classic assignment, which is also the target assignment. The classic assignment refers to topics by name. If a subscribed topic was deleted and created again with fewer partitions before the classic members rejoin, the converted members are assigned partitions of the new topic that don't exist.

Impact:
* With the uniform assignor, the default server assignor, every computation of the target assignment fails with "Partitions were left unassigned" or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
* When the assignor runs in the heartbeat, the heartbeat that converts the group fails with UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR, and every later attempt fails the same way.
* When the assignor is offloaded, every run fails, and the joining consumer never gets partitions while the converted members keep the partitions that don't exist.
* When the conversion computes no new target assignment, for example when a static member replaces its classic self with the same subscription, the members are assigned partitions that don't exist.

*Steps to reproduce*
# A classic consumer joins group G, subscribed to topic T with 4 partitions. G is Stable and the consumer is assigned T-0 to T-3.
# Delete T and create it again with 2 partitions.
# Before the classic consumer refreshes its metadata and rejoins (metadata.max.age.ms), start a consumer with group.protocol=consumer in G, subscribed to T.
# The coordinator converts G to a consumer group, and the new consumer's heartbeat fails with UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR.

*Expected:* the converted group assigns the 2 partitions of the new topic T.

summary: Do not return stale assignments in DescribeGroups for a rebalancing classic group
body:
When a classic group is in PreparingRebalance or CompletingRebalance, DescribeGroups returns the assignment of the last generation for each member. The old group coordinator returned an empty assignment and empty metadata for the members of a group that is not Stable.

The assignment of the last generation is stale during a rebalance. Eager members revoke all their partitions before they rejoin, and the next generation can move partitions to other members. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --members and Admin#describeConsumerGroups therefore show partitions for members that may no longer own them.

*Steps to reproduce*
# Start a classic consumer group G with two consumers using the range assignor, and wait until G is Stable.
# Start a third consumer, so that G starts a rebalance.
# While G rebalances, run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group G --members --verbose.

*Expected:* while G rebalances, its members show no assigned partitions, as with the old group coordinator.
*Actual:* the members show the partitions of the last generation.

summary: Add localMirrorTopicChanges method to TopicsDelta
body:
A mirror desired-state change is topic-level metadata, but it triggers work only on brokers that currently lead partitions of that topic. For this reason, we could benefit from an extra TopicsDelta filtering method that uses brokerId to filter out desired-state change for non locally led partitions. This would be useful for {{MirrorMetadataManager}}

Refer: https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/24320#discussion_r4683841834

summary: Docker image, support KRaft dynamic quorum (KIP-853) controllers
body:
The Docker image can only run controllers with static voters. With controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers instead:
 # KafkaDockerWrapper always formats with plain kafka-storage format. On a controller without voters, StorageTool requires --standalone or --no-initial-controllers, so the format fails and the container exits.
 # The image configure script rejects KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS on controller-only nodes, but a dynamic voter needs an advertised controller endpoint.

We should (i.) add a new env var (e.g. STORAGE_FORMAT_ARGS) appended to the images format command and (ii.) allow KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS on controllers when it lists only controller listeners.

Default behaviour stays unchanged. Since the env vars are part of the images, interface (KIP-975), this might require a small KIP.

Affects the 3.9.x+ version.

summary: AsyncKafkaConsumer.close() hangs indefinitely in leaveGroupOnClose when the background thread dies (e.g. OutOfMemoryError) without completing cleanup()
body:
{{AsyncKafkaConsumer.close()}} can block forever if the background {{consumer_background_thread}} ({{{}ConsumerNetworkThread{}}}) terminates abnormally.

Here are detailed analysis with the help of Kiro.

Observed sequence:
1. Application calls {{{}consumer.close(...){}}}.
2. {{close()}} → {{leaveGroupOnClose()}} enqueues a {{LeaveGroupOnCloseEvent}} via {{{}ApplicationEventHandler.addAndGet(...){}}}.
3. {{addAndGet()}} blocks in {{{}ConsumerUtils.getResult(Future){}}}, which is a bare future.get() with no timeout.
4. The {{ConsumerNetworkThread}} dies from an {{OutOfMemoryError}} that reaches its {{{}UncaughtExceptionHandler{}}}. Because of the OOM, {{ConsumerNetworkThread.cleanup()}} does not complete, so {{CompletableEventReaper.reap(applicationEventQueue)}} — the close-time safety net that completes all pending event futures exceptionally — never runs.
5. The {{LeaveGroupOnCloseEvent}} future is never completed (neither by success nor by the deadline-based {{{}TimeoutException{}}}), so the application thread parks in {{future.get()}} indefinitely.

The event does carry a deadline, but deadline enforcement lives entirely on the background thread ({{{}CompletableEventReaper{}}}). When that thread is gone, nothing enforces it, and the no-timeout {{getResult(Future)}} overload used by {{addAndGet()}} has no independent bound.

Relevant code (4.3.1, 4.4.0):
 - {{ConsumerUtils.getResult(Future)}} — return {{{}future.get(){}}}; (no timeout).
 - {{ApplicationEventHandler.addAndGet()}} — calls the no-timeout {{getResult. The {{ensureNetworkThreadAlive()}} check in {{add()}} is pre-enqueue only and documented as racy; it does not help a caller already parked in {{{}future.get(){}}}.
 - {{ConsumerNetworkThread.run()}} — relies on {{finally \{ cleanup(); } → applicationEventReaper.reap(...)}} to fail pending events, which does not survive an {{{}OutOfMemoryError{}}}.
 - {{{}AsyncKafkaConsumer.leaveGroupOnClose() / close(){}}}.

Thread dump (blocked application thread):
{code:java}
  java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
    at java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture.waitingGet(CompletableFuture.java:1919)
    at java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture.get(CompletableFuture.java:2093)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.ConsumerUtils.getResult(ConsumerUtils.java:240)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.events.ApplicationEventHandler.addAndGet(ApplicationEventHandler.java:144)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.AsyncKafkaConsumer.leaveGroupOnClose(AsyncKafkaConsumer.java:1739)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.AsyncKafkaConsumer.lambda$close$2(AsyncKafkaConsumer.java:1648)
    at org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.swallow(Utils.java:1046)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.AsyncKafkaConsumer.close(AsyncKafkaConsumer.java:1647)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.AsyncKafkaConsumer.close(AsyncKafkaConsumer.java:1558)
    at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.Kafk
comments:
Suggested fix (for discussion):
  - In ApplicationEventHandler.addAndGet(), wait using the event's deadline via the timed getResult(Future, Timer) overload instead of the unbounded getResult(Future).
  - Additionally, detect background-thread death while blocked (e.g. complete outstanding futures exceptionally when the thread terminates, or re-check networkThread.isAlive() on a bounded wait loop) so a dead thread can't strand a caller.

Hey [~abyss] , thanks for reporting this. As of 4.4 there are some validations to protect against this in the case the event is enqueued when the background thread is dead already (so should make this gap even harder to hit, needs not only the background to die, but to die after the event has been added to the queue).

I linked the Jira that added the guards to events added when the background thread is dead fail fast.

All that being said, I agree that we could still hit the hang you describe, if an event is added to the queue and then the background thread dies. Some thoughts for when looking into fixing here:
 * I expect the hang in that edge case would affect other APIs (not only close). All Apis that rely on the background thread reaping/expiring the events
 * we should me mindful about any change we add to fix this edge case (e.g., careful not to break the expiration logic driven by the background, or to add overhead on the inter-thread communication that we've seen it can easily affect CPU)

Happy to help with reviews if you or someone else takes on this. Thanks!

summary: Streams client can report an active task's offset without its end offset after the task finished restoring
body:
Under the streams group protocol, a client reports the changelog offsets of the active tasks it is restoring, and their end offsets. The coordinator treats an active task with a reported offset as restoring. With an end offset, it can tell whether the task is caught up.

The client computes the two values on different threads:
 * TaskManager.maybeUpdateTaskOffsetSumSnapshot() runs on the stream thread, once per runOnce(). It reports the offset of every assigned task that is not RUNNING.
 * DefaultStateUpdater.updateTaskEndOffsetSumSnapshot() runs on the state updater thread, once per loop. It computes end offsets only for the tasks the state updater is still restoring or updating.

Once the state updater completes an active task's restore, it drops the task's end offset right away. The task's offset stays in the stream thread's snapshot until that thread recomputes the snapshot after taking over the restored task. In between, the client reports the task with an offset and without an end offset. The coordinator sees the owner as restoring with an unknown lag. The warm-up refiner then counts the owner's state as not usable, and moves the task cold when the target assignment gives it to another member.

The gap lasts as long as the stream thread is busy, for example processing a record that takes long or running a punctuation. The heartbeat thread keeps sending the stale offset in the meantime.

summary: Kafka Streams may report stales changelog endOffsets during "active-restore" phase
body:
With the new "streams" rebalance protocol, Kafka Streams reports task-offset and task-end-offset information to the broker for standby/warmup tasks. However, if an active task needs to get restored, the state-updater-thread pauses to update standby/warmup tasks, as long as it's restoring the active task (this could take a longer period of time). During this phase, both task-offset and task-end-offset freeze. While this is correct for task-offset, it's incorrect for task-end-offset because the active task on some other member would still append new data to the changelog. (The freeze happens, because we currently update the task-end-offset information only based on the fetched record batches, which is "for free", ie does not require any additional RPC). As a side effect, the broker only sees incorrect lag information for these standby/warmup task over time (the observed lag is frozen while the real lag grows). If the last report told the broker that the standby/warmup is hot (ie, lag below acceptable.recovery.lag), the broker might incorrectly promote the standby/warmup to active in a rebalance or refiner stop even if the task did cool down in the mean time.

To fix this issue, we should send explicit "get endOffset" request to the broker to refresh the task-end-offset correctly, for the pause partition as long as the state-updater is in "active restoring" phase (when we transit back to "standby updating" mode, we don't need the additional RPCs).

The streams heartbeat thread sends a task-(end)-offset update only every 60sec by default (task offset reporting interval config), and thus we only need to send additional RPCs rarely enough that it's not a performance concern. We need to avoid blocking the state-updater-thread and should use a short RPC timeout – failures can be ignored (and can lead to reporting "unknown"), because we would retry after 60seconds again anyway.

summary: Consider scheduling the share group assignor when share partitions are initialized
body:
With assignor offloading on, a new share group's first assignor run is scheduled before its share partitions are initialized, so that run assigns nothing. The partitions are only assigned after the next heartbeat bumps the group epoch and a second run completes. That costs members an extra heartbeat (see ShareConsumerCallbackTest.testAcknowledgementSentOnSubscriptionChange).

Bump the group epoch and schedule the assignor run in initializeShareGroupState instead, so the second heartbeat already receives the assignment.

https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/24319 will add a test scenario for this. Please wait until that PR has been merged before starting this work.
comments:
Hi [~squah-confluent], now that PR #24319 has merged, I'd like to pick this up if you haven't already started on it.

Reading through the offloading path, bumping the group epoch and scheduling a run from {{initializeShareGroupState}} doesn't seem to be enough on its own in two cases:

# The first run has already installed its empty assignment. With the default 1000 ms value for {{group.share.assignment.interval.ms}}, {{canComputeNextTargetAssignment}} returns false if initialization finishes less than 1000 ms after the empty assignment was computed. ({{testShareGroupAsyncTargetAssignmentWithPartitionInitialization}} sets the interval to 0, so it doesn't hit this.) I think the initialization path needs to bypass the interval.
# The first run is still in flight, as in that test. Bumping to the next epoch doesn't cancel it, because {{maybeCancelStaleTargetAssignmentUpdate}} only cancels runs at or above the new epoch, and no new run can be scheduled while one is in flight. I'd cancel it explicitly and schedule a replacement for the new epoch.

For the implementation, I'm thinking of extracting the scheduling logic from {{maybeUpdateTargetAssignment}} so {{initializeShareGroupState}} can call it without a heartbeating member. I'd pass the updated set of initialized partitions into the group spec explicitly, since the initialization record hasn't been replayed at that point.

Does that approach sound reasonable? In particular, is it OK for the initialization path to bypass the interval?

Hi [~sunm2n], the ticket can be picked up.

We shouldn't bypass the interval or cancel existing runs. If you wish to pick up the ticket, these questions need consideration:
# What if we skip the first empty assignment instead when a fresh group has no initialized partitions?
# What happens if we are initializing 100 partitions and the initializations come in slowly over time?
## Is there actually a difference in the total number of heartbeats needed when assignment batching and/or offloading are enabled?
# What happens if a new member joins an existing group with an extra topic subscription?
# Based on the answer to 2.1, does the premise of this ticket even make sense?
## If not, is there an alternative proposal that would improve the number of heartbeats until the group is fully stable?

We also should not split {{maybeUpdateTargetAssignment}}. We can check how streams groups handles starting an assignment once the initial rebalance delay has elapsed.

summary: KRaft observers busy-poll when no voter responds
body:
When an observer (e.g. a broker) gets no response from any voter, the KRaft I/O thread busy-loops: {{KafkaRaftClient.poll()}} computes a poll timeout of 0 on every iteration until a leader responds. This happens in two states.

*Follower*
{{maybeSendFetchToBestNode()}} returns {{min(backoffMs, state.remainingFetchTimeMs(currentTimeMs))}}. Only a successful fetch resets the fetch timer, so once the fetch timeout expires the result is always 0. Voters transition to prospective when the fetch timeout expires. Observers have had no such transition since KAFKA-19354 removed the observer's fetch-timeout branch, so they stay in the follower state and spin.

*Unattached*
An observer that starts up unattached ({{QuorumState.initialize()}}) gets a finite election timeout ({{randomElectionTimeoutMs()}}). Later transitions to unattached give observers {{Long.MAX_VALUE}}. {{pollUnattachedCommon()}} returns {{min(fetchBackoffMs, state.remainingElectionTimeMs(currentTimeMs))}}, so once the election timeout expires the result is always 0. Observers never act on the election timeout.

*Impact*
A busy loop on the raft I/O thread while the controller quorum is unavailable. Profiles show it as a significant share of broker CPU in {{FollowerState.leaderNode}}, {{VoterSet.isVoter}} and {{RequestManager.hasAnyInflightRequest}}.

*Proposed fix*
Bound the poll timeout by the fetch and election timeouts only on the voter paths ({{pollFollowerAsVoter}}, {{pollUnattachedAsVoter}}), since only voters act on them. Observers then wait for the in-flight fetch or the bootstrap server backoff.
