summary: Add rack-aware standby task assignment
body:
In the "classic" protocol, there is "sticky" and "ha_assignor" options, and KIP-1071 defines both assignor options, too. The "sticky" assignor is already available, while the "ha_assignor" is missing.

However, KIP-1071 introduced a different architecture and the class HA-assignor features are not delivered in the same way, instead, "warmup tasks" are injected via a new refiner step, and the HA-assignor does not need to concern itself with it.

The HA-assignor also computes a different assignment compare to "sticky", which we are tracking via it's own sub-task.

This ticket is about adding rack-aware standby task assignment, to make KIP-1017 feature complete with the classic HA-assignor (note, that the classic sticky assignor does not implement rack-aware standby task assignment). To this end, we want to not only close this "ha" feature gap, but implement rack-aware standby task assignment for both "sticky" and "balance" assignor.

summary: Consumer and Streams group leave append failures can lose session timers and stall reassignment
body:
When a member using {{group.protocol=consumer}} or {{group.protocol=streams}} leaves its group, the coordinator cancels the member’s session timer before persisting the member removal records.

If the subsequent local append to {{__consumer_offsets}} fails, the coordinator’s snapshot rollback restores the member metadata, existing assignment, and ownership state. However, session timers are not managed by the snapshot mechanism, so the canceled timer is not restored.

As a result, the coordinator retains a member that has already shut down as the owner of Consumer partitions or Streams active tasks, but no longer has a session timer to expire that member. Even after the append failure is resolved and other members continue sending successful heartbeats, the departed member’s partitions or tasks may remain unreleased, leaving processing stalled.

The two protocols use different leave handlers, but share the same underlying cause: timers are canceled before persistence and are not restored on rollback.

 

*Scenario*
 # Dynamic members A and B belong to the same group, with stable assignments. In a Consumer group, A consumes P0 and B consumes P1. In a Streams group, A and B belong to different processes: A processes active task {{{}0_0{}}}, and B processes active task {{{}0_1{}}}.
 # A shuts down and sends a heartbeat with {{memberEpoch=-1}} using the corresponding protocol. A sends no further heartbeats. For Streams, this is an ordinary member departure without requesting application-wide shutdown.
 # The coordinator generates A’s removal records and a group epoch update record, then calls {{cancelTimers()}} to cancel A’s timers before persisting the records.
 # The local append of the batch containing these records fails. The coordinator remains ACTIVE without reloading and performs a snapshot rollback.
 # A’s member metadata and existing partition or active task ownership are restored, but A’s session timer is not.
 # The cause of the append failure is resolved. B continues sending successful heartbeats and processing its existing partitions or tasks, but B’s heartbeats refresh only B’s own session timer.
 # A is not removed even after its session timeout has elapsed. Consumption of P0 remains stalled in the Consumer group, or processing of task {{0_0}} remains stalled in the Streams group.

Even if a subsequent rebalance changes the target assignment to move the affected partition or task to B, B may be unable to acquire it while the coordinator still retains A’s current ownership.

For Streams, this scenario does not require a stateful topology, standby or warm-up replicas, or a custom assignor.

 

*Conditions that can cause the append failure*

One possible path is a reduction of {{max.message.bytes}} for {{__consumer_offsets}} between batch creation and append. Both group types use the same coordinator runtime persistence path, so this condition applies to both.

The coordinator runtime uses the size limit in effect when creating a batch. I

summary: KRaft follower stays out of sync after recovery with conflicting records in the same leader epoch
body:
h3. Observed behavior

Observed on Apache Kafka 4.2.1 in KRaft mode (commit {{18d5ecd939c8d510}}). After an unclean shutdown, a restarting broker recovered a shorter local log for a partition of {{__consumer_offsets}}. It applied its previous leader assignment while registration was pending and its group coordinator appended a new group metadata record at the recovered log end.

Selected Kafka log excerpts below are abridged. Broker, group and partition identifiers and wall-clock timestamps are omitted. {{N}} stands for the same offset throughout and {{E}} stands for the same leader epoch.

{code}
INFO Unable to register broker <broker> because the controller returned error DUPLICATE_BROKER_REGISTRATION
INFO Publishing initial metadata ...
INFO Recovering ... since no clean shutdown file was found
INFO Completed load of Log(... logEndOffset=N ...)
INFO Scheduling loading of metadata from __consumer_offsets-<partition> with epoch E
INFO Group <group> with generation <generation> is now empty.
{code}

The decoded batches at the same position contained different records. Both batches passed checksum validation and both carried epoch {{E}}.

{code}
Replica          Epoch  Base offset  Last offset  Record at N
Restarted copy   E      N            N            GroupMetadata (members=[])
Leader copy      E      N            N+3          OffsetCommit
{code}

On the next startup the broker registered, reopened the same local log and became a follower. Its next fetch offset was {{N+1}}. The leader's epoch checkpoint showed the exclusive end of {{E}} at {{N+10}}. The request was within that epoch on the leader, which is consistent with the history check proceeding without truncation. The leader returned the whole batch containing {{N+1}}, beginning at {{N}}. The follower rejected the overlap.

{code}
org.apache.kafka.server.storage.log.UnexpectedAppendOffsetException:
Unexpected offset in append to __consumer_offsets-<partition>.
First offset N is less than the next offset N+1.
WARN Partition __consumer_offsets-<partition> marked as failed
{code}

Two partitions showed this pattern. Restarting the follower again repeated the failure. Removing and then re-adding its replica through partition reassignment rebuilt the local copy and restored ISR membership.

h3. Expected behavior

A restarting replica should be able to resume replication from a consistent log. Please investigate whether internal group writes should be gated while registration is pending, and how follower recovery should handle conflicting records with the same offset and epoch.

The exact reason the first recovered log was shorter and an isolated reproduction remain unverified.

summary: Admin client metadata refresh uses a flat retry.backoff.ms when the response lacks the node a pending call needs
body:
When a metadata request fails, the admin client retries it with exponential backoff and jitter, bounded by \{{retry.backoff.max.ms}} ([KafkaAdminClient.java#L989|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/admin/KafkaAdminClient.java#L989]).

There is no such backoff when the metadata request succeeds but the response doesn't contain the node that a pending call needs. Examples are a call that targets a specific broker id (such as \{{describeConfigs}} for a broker, or \{{describeLogDirs}}) while that broker is not in the metadata, or a call that needs the controller when none is present. The node provider requests another metadata update and leaves the call pending ([KafkaAdminClient.java#L822-L833|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/admin/KafkaAdminClient.java#L822-L833]). \{{AdminMetadataManager}} then waits a fixed \{{retry.backoff.ms}} before the next attempt ([AdminMetadataManager.java#L298-L301|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/admin/internals/AdminMetadataManager.java#L298-L301]). It doesn't take \{{retry.backoff.max.ms}} into account ([KafkaAdminClient.java#L583-L586|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/admin/KafkaAdminClient.java#L583-L586]), and the delay doesn't grow across attempts.

As a result, the client sends a Metadata request every \{{retry.backoff.ms}} (100 ms by default) until the pending call times out (\{{default.api.timeout.ms}}, 60 s by default).

The producer and consumer already back off exponentially in the equivalent situation, where metadata responses succeed but make no progress (\{{equivalentResponseCount}} in [Metadata.java#L154-L168|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/clients/Metadata.java#L154-L168]).

h3. Suggested change

When successive metadata responses don't change the cluster view, \{{AdminMetadataManager}} should apply exponential backoff with jitter, bounded by \{{retry.backoff.max.ms}}, to the next refresh. The backoff should reset once a response makes progress. This matches the existing documentation of \{{retry.backoff.max.ms}} and the behaviour of \{{Metadata}}, and needs no new config.

summary: Upgrading a Stable classic group by static member replacement leaves partitions unassigned
body:
When a static member of a Stable classic group restarts with the consumer protocol, the same group.instance.id and the same subscription, the group is upgraded to a consumer group that takes the last classic assignment as its target assignment. If a partition of a subscribed topic is in no member's assignment at that time, the consumer group leaves it unassigned until an unrelated change bumps the group epoch: a member joins, leaves or changes its subscription, or a subscribed topic changes again. Nobody consumes the partition in the meantime. A rolling upgrade of static members restarts every member this way, so the partition can stay unassigned after the upgrade has completed.

A Stable classic group has such partitions:
* After its topic gained partitions, until the classic leader sees them and rejoins.
* With the cooperative protocol, while a partition moves to another member: it is revoked in one generation and only assigned in the next one, after the members rejoin.

The classic members that rejoin with the same subscription, including the leader that sees the new partitions, do not bump the group epoch of the consumer group, and neither does the metadata refresh of the coordinator.

*Steps to reproduce*
# Two classic consumers with group.instance.id B and A and the cooperative-sticky assignor join group G in this order, subscribed to topic T with 2 partitions. G is Stable and B is the leader.
# Add 2 partitions to T.
# Before B refreshes its metadata (metadata.max.age.ms), restart consumer A with group.protocol=consumer, the same group.instance.id and the same subscription. The default group.consumer.migration.policy allows the upgrade.
# The coordinator upgrades G to a consumer group. T-2 and T-3 are in no member's assignment.
# ConsumerGroupDescribe shows T-2 and T-3 in no member's assignment, and they stay unassigned after B refreshes its metadata and rejoins.

*Expected:* the upgraded group assigns every partition of its subscribed topics.

summary: Add opt-in per-principal remote storage fetch metrics (KIP-1404)
body: With Tiered Storage, the broker exposes remote fetch metrics only per topic and per broker [KIP-963|https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/263426481/KIP-963+Additional+metrics+in+Tiered+Storage], so operators cannot tell which principal is reading from remote storage or from which topic. This adds opt-in metrics keyed by authenticated principal and topic, with optional client-id: remote-fetch-byte-rate/total and remote-fetch-request-rate/total under kafka.server:type=remote-fetch-principal-metrics. It is disabled by default (remote.fetch.principal.metrics.enable), with idle keys expiring after remote.fetch.principal.metrics.ttl.ms. Details are in the KIP: https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/467436009/Per-Principal+Remote+Storage+Fetch+Metrics

summary: Replace the range assignor with range assignor v2
Align partitions with the racks of their consumers in the range2 assignor
Add a fuzzer for the range2 assignor
Add a sticky range assignor, without rack awareness
Range v2: make the range assignor sticky
body:
The range assignor, the server-side assignor of consumer groups (KIP-848) that keeps co-partitioned topics together, computes every assignment from scratch. It sorts the members and cuts every topic into consecutive ranges in that order. When a member joins or leaves, the ranges of the other members shift, so partitions move between members that did not change.

For example, take three members A, B and C subscribed to a topic T of twelve partitions, and a fourth member D that joins:

||Member||Before||Range assignor, after D joins||Moving only what D needs||
|A|T-0, T-1, T-2, T-3|T-0, T-1, T-2|T-0, T-1, T-2|
|B|T-4, T-5, T-6, T-7|T-3, T-4, T-5|T-4, T-5, T-6|
|C|T-8, T-9, T-10, T-11|T-6, T-7, T-8|T-8, T-9, T-10|
|D| |T-9, T-10, T-11|T-3, T-7, T-11|

D needs three partitions. The range assignor moves six: T-3 goes from A to B, and T-6 and T-7 from B to C, although neither B nor C changed. Every co-partitioned topic moves the same way. With 30 members and a topic of 1,200 partitions, a join moves about 430 partitions where 38 are enough, and a rolling restart of the group moves every partition several times. Every moved partition is revoked from a member that is consuming it, which commits its offsets and gives up its state, and is then fetched again by another member.

The range assignor also gives the extra partitions of every topic, those left when its partitions do not divide evenly, to the first members in its order. With three members and topics of 4, 5, 7, 8, 10 and 11 partitions, the members get 18, 15 and 12 partitions where 15 each is possible. Finally, it ignores racks, where the client-side range assignor aligns partitions with the racks of the consumers, and it builds a new assignment for every member on every run, even when nothing changes.

The goal is a new version of the range assignor, meant to replace it, with these properties in priority order:

# *Validity*: every partition of every subscribed topic goes to exactly one of its subscribers.
# *Spread*: every subscriber of a topic gets the same number of its partitions, or one more.
# *Co-partitioning*: topics with the same subscribers and the same number of partitions are assigned together. Every member gets the same partitions of all of them, as with the range assignor today.
# *Balance*: the extra partitions are spread over the members instead of going to the first ones, as far as co-partitioning allows.
# *Rack alignment*, when enabled: as many partitions as possible go to a member in a rack holding one of their replicas, without breaking the properties above.
# *Stickiness*: partitions move only when the properties above require it, and an assignment that already has them stays unchanged. A join moves about what the joiner gets, and a leave about what the leaver had.
# *Determinism*: the assignment only depends on the group and its topics, not on the order in which they are given.

The new version reuses the uniform assignor v2 (KAFKA-21163): topics with the same subscribers a

summary: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expired
body:
Code inspection found that a group heartbeat manager can return a zero poll timeout
while a heartbeat request is still in flight.

When the heartbeat timer expires, \{{HeartbeatRequestState.timeToNextHeartbeatMs()}}
falls through to the remaining retry backoff. That backoff is measured from the last
response, so it is normally already 0. The heartbeat managers propagate this value
through \{{poll()}} and \{{maximumTimeToWait()}}, so the network and application threads
busy loop until the response arrives or the request times out.

This happens after the member has joined (typically \{{STABLE}}). The client has
learned the heartbeat interval and sent a later heartbeat, but the response does not
arrive before that interval elapses. The heartbeat timer expires while the request
remains in flight, and the request has not yet reached \{{request.timeout.ms}}.

The fix is to return the initial retry backoff in this state. It applies to the
consumer, share and streams heartbeat managers because they share
{\{HeartbeatRequestState}}.

Out of scope:
* The first heartbeat while joining is covered by KAFKA-19804, which starts the
  heartbeat timer with \{{request.timeout.ms}} as the interval.
* \{{retry.backoff.ms=0}} still results in a zero wait. This is tracked consistently
  across the request managers in KAFKA-21049.

summary: kafka-streams-groups --describe --offsets prints nothing for an Empty streams group
body:
For a streams group in the Empty state, kafka-streams-groups.sh --describe --group <g> --offsets prints no output and exits with code 0, even though the group still has committed offsets.
The cause is that StreamsGroupCommand#getOffsets collects partitions only from live members' active-task assignments, and printOffsets only runs when the group has more than 0 members, so even the "has no active members" message never prints.
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe shows committed offsets for Empty groups, so the streams tool behaves differently.
Fix: when the group has no members, read the partitions from the group's committed offsets for its source and repartition topics, print them with their lag, and print the "no active members" notice to stderr.
Current workaround: --reset-offsets --all-input-topics --to-current --dry-run --export.

summary: Improve kafka-streams-groups --describe offsets output
body:
For a partition with no committed offset, kafka-streams-groups --describe --offsets reports lag as log-end offset minus log-start offset (StreamsGroupCommand#getOffsets), as if the app had started from the earliest offset. The default view shows only OFFSET-LAG, so "never committed" looks the same as "behind by N".

Offset rows also have no member, process or client-id columns and are not sorted, and there is no "group is rebalancing" warning or explanation of what the NotReady state means.
kafka-consumer-groups --describe shows - for current offset and lag when nothing is committed, shows CURRENT-OFFSET and LOG-END-OFFSET by default, lists each partition's owner, and warns when a group is rebalancing.

Fix: print - for current offset and lag when nothing is committed, show current and log-end offsets by default, add owner columns (- when unowned), sort rows by topic and partition, and print warnings for rebalancing and NotReady groups.
Found while comparing with kafka-consumer-groups; affects 4.1.0+ (--describe was added in KAFKA-18288).

summary: Fix kafka-streams-groups --reset-offsets --input-topic and help text
body:
kafka-streams-groups --reset-offsets --input-topic T only works if every partition of T already has a committed offset in the group (StreamsGroupCommand#filterExistingGroupTopics). Otherwise it prints "One or more topics are not part of the group", resets nothing, and still exits 0.

This blocks resets after partitions are added to an input topic, when only some partitions were committed, and when pre-loading a new application.id by topic with --to-earliest or --to-datetime (only --from-file works). kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets --topic has no such restriction.

Separately, the --reset-offsets help text says --execute deletes all internal topics, but they are only deleted with --delete-all-internal-topics or --delete-internal-topic, so users may keep stale changelogs.

Fix: accept any input topic of the group's topology and reset all its partitions, exit non-zero when nothing is reset, and correct the help text.

Found while comparing with kafka-consumer-groups; affects 4.2.0+ (reset-offsets was added in KAFKA-19244).

summary: KafkaStreams.removeStreamThread can deadlock with a concurrent REPLACE_THREAD uncaught-exception handler
body:
KafkaStreams.removeStreamThread(long) holds the changeThreadCount monitor across a StreamThread.waitOnThreadState(DEAD, ...) call. If the removal target happens to be the same StreamThread that concurrently entered the REPLACE_THREAD uncaught-exception handler, the whole client deadlocks and no further threads can be added, removed, or replaced.

The affected KafkaStreams client stays alive (JVM/GC keeps ticking) but its Streams pipeline stops making progress indefinitely.


The paths that collide

KafkaStreams.removeStreamThread(long):

    synchronized (changeThreadCount) {                                // holds lock
KafkaStreams.removeStreamThread(long) holds the changeThreadCount monitor across a StreamThread.waitOnThreadState(DEAD, ...) call. If the removal target happens to be the same StreamThread that concurrently entered the REPLACE_THREAD uncaught-exception handler, the whole client deadlocks and no further threads can be added, removed, or replaced.

The affected KafkaStreams client stays alive (JVM/GC keeps ticking) but its Streams pipeline stops making progress indefinitely.


The paths that collide

```

KafkaStreams.removeStreamThread(long):

    synchronized (changeThreadCount) {                                // holds lock
        ...
        streamThread.shutdown(GroupMembershipOperation.LEAVE_GROUP);  // signals target
        if (callingThreadIsNotCurrentStreamThread) {
            ...
            if (!streamThread.waitOnThreadState(State.DEAD, remainingTimeMs)) { // BLOCKS while still holding the lock
                ...
            }
        }
    }

KafkaStreams.addStreamThread() (also the tail of replaceStreamThread, which the REPLACE_THREAD uncaught-exception handler calls):

    synchronized (changeThreadCount) \{ ... }

```


Deadlock scenario

Two callers, one soak-style scheduleAtFixedRate loop that calls removeStreamThread(), and a StreamThread that throws an exception the uncaught-exception handler maps to REPLACE_THREAD:

1. The scheduler thread enters synchronized (changeThreadCount) inside removeStreamThread, iterates threads, picks StreamThread-N, calls streamThread.shutdown(...) (which only sets state to PENDING_SHUTDOWN), then blocks in waitOnThreadState(DEAD, ...) still holding the lock.

2. StreamThread-N's current runOnce invocation throws. The uncaught handler returns REPLACE_THREAD, which calls replaceStreamThread(...) -> deadThread.shutdown() -> addStreamThread(). That method also needs synchronized (changeThreadCount), so StreamThread-N blocks trying to reacquire the lock.

3. setState(DEAD) fires only at the end of completeShutdown(), which StreamThread-N can reach only by returning from the uncaught-exception handler and out of run(). It cannot, because it is blocked on changeThreadCount.

4. The scheduler thread waits forever for a DEAD transition that never comes.

If the removal target is a different StreamThread than the one that hit the exception, no deadlock: that thread's completeShutdown does

summary: Transaction coordinator could return INVALID_TXN_STATE from stale cache after losing __transaction_state leadership
body:
When a broker loses leadership of a __transaction_state partition, there is a *race* between the replica state change and the transaction coordinator's resignation. BrokerMetadataPublisher.onMetadataUpdate applies the delta to ReplicaManager first, which makes the broker a follower. It then updates the group coordinator, and only after that calls TransactionCoordinator.onResignation, which drops the partition's entry from the TransactionStateManager cache. Until resignation runs, the broker is a follower for the partition but still answers coordinator requests from its old cache. The window is usually short, but its length depends on how much work the publish does before it reaches the transaction coordinator, and it can stretch to seconds.

TransactionStateManager.getAndMaybeAddTransactionState only checks loadingPartitions and transactionMetadataCache; it never checks that the broker still leads the partition. Answers that require a log write are safe: the acks=-1 append fails with NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER, which is mapped to NOT_COORDINATOR. Answers decided purely from the cache are not, so any request that hits the old coordinator inside the window can get a wrong answer.

{*}With TV2{*}, one way to lose this race is a fatal producer error:
1. Transaction N commits on coordinator A. A's cache holds COMPLETE_COMMIT at epoch E, and the client now has epoch E.
2. Leadership of the __transaction_state partition moves to broker B. B loads the partition, and the partition leaders' implicit AddPartitionsToTxn for transaction N+1 go to B, which moves the transaction to ONGOING.
3. The client has had no reason to rediscover the coordinator: under TV2, EndTxn is its first coordinator request in the transaction. So it sends EndTxn(COMMIT, E) to A.
4. If this request reaches A after A became a follower but before it resigned, A answers from its cache. COMPLETE_COMMIT + COMMIT at the current epoch is not a retry, so A returns INVALID_TXN_STATE without writing to the log:
TransactionalId: <id>'s state is COMPLETE_COMMIT, but received transaction marker result to send: COMMIT
5. The producer treats INVALID_TXN_STATE as fatal. The transaction on B stays ONGOING until it times out (or the producer re-initializes).

If the EndTxn arrives after A resigns, A returns NOT_COORDINATOR, and the client rediscovers B and commits normally. The outcome depends only on which side of that window the request lands. It doesn't need a broker pause or any fault: an ordinary leadership move (reassignment, controlled shutdown, preferred leader election) is enough, and producers that commit often are the most exposed.

Other answers decided purely from the cache race the same way, for example PRODUCER_FENCED / INVALID_PRODUCER_ID_MAPPING, the verify-only AddPartitionsToTxn path, and the "partitions already added" shortcut.

summary: LogManager#loadLog leaves kafka.log:type=Log gauges registered for stray log directories
comments:
Correction to the "Suggested fix" in the description: calling {{removeLogMetrics()}} in the stray branches of {{loadLog}} is not safe on its own.

Log gauges are registered under a name built only from {{topic}} and {{partition}} ({{UnifiedLog#newMetrics}}), and Yammer's {{newGauge}} keeps the gauge that is already registered for a name. When a stray directory and a live replica of the same partition are loaded, whichever {{UnifiedLog}} is created first owns the series, and the other one's registration is silently ignored. {{removeMetric}} removes by name, so the stray log removing its "own" metrics also removes the live replica's.

I confirmed this with a test on trunk (b2ab2389a8): load a live replica, load a copy of its directory as {{<topic>-0.<id>-stray}} through {{loadLog}}, call {{removeLogMetrics()}} on the returned stray log. All five {{kafka.log:type=Log}} gauges of the live partition are gone afterwards ("live replica metrics lost: []"). So the naive fix would turn wrong values into missing metrics for the live replica, which is worse.

A correct fix needs the stray decision to happen before any gauge is registered:
* for {{*-stray}} directories the name is known up front, so no {{UnifiedLog}} (or at least no metrics) needs to be created for them;
* for the {{isStray}} predicate the decision needs the topic id read inside the {{UnifiedLog}} constructor, so metric registration would have to move out of the constructor, or the check would have to run before the log is created.

The second point overlaps with KAFKA-20567, which already proposes deciding "stray" before {{UnifiedLog#create}}. If that goes in, the {{isStray}} case of this report is covered, and what remains is the {{*-stray}} directory case plus the {{-delete}} case I mentioned (not verified). I would like to avoid a conflicting change, so happy to follow whatever direction the KAFKA-20567 assignee and the maintainers prefer.

summary: A Streams static rejoin rejected by topology validation causes a subsequent valid rejoin to receive an empty task assignment
body:
When a Streams static member’s rejoin is rejected by topology validation, changes made to the intermediate assignment cache can remain. A subsequent member rejoining with the correct topology can therefore receive an empty assignment in its first response, even though the previous task assignment is available for inheritance.

*Scenario*
 # Static member A is operating normally and owns task T. The coordinator has an intermediate assignment cached for the current assignment epoch.
 # A temporarily leaves the group normally ({{{}memberEpoch=-2{}}}). The coordinator preserves its member information and target assignment so they can be inherited upon rejoining.
 # Before the session expires, B rejoins with A’s instance ID and a new member ID. Due to a deployment error, for example, B submits different topology contents while retaining the existing topology epoch.
 # While preparing the static member replacement, the coordinator changes the intermediate assignment cache key from A to B. It then detects the topology mismatch and rejects B’s request with {{{}STREAMS_INVALID_TOPOLOGY_EPOCH{}}}.
 # B’s member replacement is not applied, so the stored member and target assignment still refer to A. However, the intermediate assignment cache retains B’s key.
 # Before the session expires, C rejoins with the original topology restored, the same instance ID and process ID, and a new member ID. The relevant topology epoch, metadata, and assignment configuration remain unchanged.
 # C’s rejoin succeeds, but the coordinator cannot find A’s cached entry to transfer to C. The first response therefore contains an empty active assignment instead of task T.

Without B’s rejected join attempt, C receives the existing task T in its first rejoin response. The cache mutation from the rejected request changes the outcome of a subsequent valid request.
comments:
Thanks for filing this ticket.

We noted the same issue on PR #24166: relabelRefinedAssignment runs in getOrMaybeCreateStaticStreamsGroupMember, before the last throws in the heartbeat handler, and isn't rolled back. Besides the topology mismatch (maybeUpdateTopology), throwIfRequestContainsInvalidTasks can also reject the request after the relabel. A retry with the same member ID heals; a rejoin with a new member ID gets an empty assignment until the next epoch bump.

Suggested fix: move the relabel into the handler after the last throw, using replaceStaticOldMember.

Do you want to pickup working on a fix? If not, [~lucasbru] or I would want to pick it up.

[~mjsax] 

Thanks for taking the time to look into this.
I'm happy to work on the fix.

summary: Avoid out of order sequence errors from multiple in-flight batches
body:
Consider a similar setup to KAFKA-9199:

The broker attempts to cache the state of the last 5 batches in order to enable duplicate detection. It is possible in some cases for this to result in a sequence such as the following:
 # Send batch n
 # Batch n successfully written, but response is delayed
 # Send batch n+1, receive successful response for n+1
 # Send batch n+2, receive successful response for n+2
 # Send batch n+3, receive successful response for n+3
 # Send batch n+4, receive successful response for n+4
 # Send batch n+5, receive successful response for n+5
 # Batch n times out, or we receive a {{NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER}} response
 # Retry batch n, the response is {{OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE}}, retry again and again

This situation could happen with a {{max.in.flight.requests.per.connection}} as low as 2.

To avoid this situation, we can avoid putting batch n+5 in flight while batch n is in flight when idempotency is enabled.

summary: Improved changelog config documentation
body:
TLDR: Global topic.* configs do not override retention.ms for windowed changelog topics or min.compaction.lag.ms for versioned changelog topics. We should document this explicitly.

Long version:

Internal topic configs are merged in three layers: type defaults < global topic.* configs < per-store configs (withLoggingEnabled(Map)). This is stated in the code comment in each InternalTopicConfig#properties() and in the docs ("Override default for both changelog and repartition topics", config-streams.md).

Two values do not follow this rule:
 * windowed changelog: retention.ms = store retention + windowstore.changelog.additional.retention.ms
 * versioned changelog: min.compaction.lag.ms = history retention + 24h (hard-coded)

Both are written _after_ the merge, unless the _per-store_ map contains the key. A global topic.retention.ms / topic.min.compaction.lag.ms is overwritten without any message.

 
{code:java}
// WindowedChangelogTopicConfig#properties()
topicConfig.putAll(defaultProperties);   // global topic.*
topicConfig.putAll(topicConfigs);        // per-store
if (!topicConfigs.containsKey(TopicConfig.RETENTION_MS_CONFIG)) {  // checks per-store map only
    topicConfig.put(TopicConfig.RETENTION_MS_CONFIG, ...);          // overwrites global value
}
{code}
VersionedChangelogTopicConfig#properties() does the same for min.compaction.lag.ms.

 

A per-store value replaces the derived value as given, with no additional retention or compaction lag added.

This applies to both group.protocol=classic and group.protocol=streams: the merge happens on the client for both.

The behavior itself is reasonable: a single global value cannot fit stores with different retention periods, and a value that is too small loses data when the store restores. But it is not documented, and the code comment states the opposite.

Suggested fix:
 * Document the exception (docs + topic.* prefix Javadoc), and correct the code comments.
 * Log a WARN when a global topic.retention.ms / topic.min.compaction.lag.ms is ignored for a store.
 * Extend test coverage for these case in InternalTopicConfigTest

*Side finding:* VersionedKeyValueStoreIntegrationTest sets TopicConfig.MIN_COMPACTION_LAG_MS_CONFIG _without_ the topic. prefix. The comment there says it is meant to "prevent premature compaction ... while using timestamped store". But both places that read topic configs (StreamThread.java:745, InternalTopicManager.java:119) only use originalsWithPrefix(TOPIC_PREFIX), so the setting never reaches the changelog.

summary: Connect: altered/reset source connector offsets can be overwritten by a task that is still being stopped on another worker
body:
With incremental cooperative rebalancing and exactly-once source support disabled, a request to alter or reset the offsets of a stopped source connector (KIP-875) can succeed while a task of that connector is still running on a non-leader worker. When that task is stopped a moment later, its final offset commit overwrites the offsets written by the request.

h3. How to reproduce

* 1 broker, 3 distributed Connect workers (apache/kafka:4.3.1), connect.protocol=sessioned (default), exactly.once.source.support=disabled (default)
* A FileStreamSourceConnector reading a file that is continuously appended to, with its task running on a worker that is not the leader
* Against the leader:
** PUT /connectors/\{name\}/stop
** PATCH /connectors/\{name\}/offsets with position 0, immediately after the stop request returns (retry on 409)
** GET /connectors/\{name\}/offsets a few seconds later

Result on 4.3.1: the PATCH returns 200 after 40-50 ms without a single 409, a GET right after it returns position 0, but 8 seconds later the stored position is the one committed by the stopped task. This happened in 10 out of 10 runs. When the task is on the leader the problem does not occur, because the leader stops its own tasks on the herder thread before it processes the request.

h3. Cause

{{DistributedHerder#modifyConnectorOffsetsChecks}} accepts the request when no rebalance is pending, the target state is STOPPED and the connector has zero task configs. The comment there says that under these conditions "we can be sure that the tasks have at least been attempted to be stopped".

That does not hold for tasks owned by other workers. With incremental cooperative rebalancing, the rebalance that follows the stop request only delivers the revocation to the owning worker. The worker stops the revoked tasks after it has received the assignment and then rejoins the group. On the leader, {{needsReconfigRebalance}} is already cleared at that point and no rebalance is pending until the worker rejoins, so the check passes while the task is still running.

With exactly-once source support enabled this is covered by the round of zombie fencing that precedes the offset write. Without it there is nothing that keeps the still-running task from committing.

h3. Proposed fix

The leader already knows which tasks it asked workers to revoke in the last rebalance ({{IncrementalCooperativeAssignor.ClusterAssignment#newlyRevokedTasks}}). A worker that was asked to revoke tasks rejoins only after it has stopped them, and that rejoin triggers the next rebalance, which replaces the leader state.

So the leader can keep the set of connectors that had tasks revoked in the most recent rebalance in {{WorkerCoordinator.LeaderState}} and reject offset modification requests for those source connectors with a {{RebalanceNeededException}} (HTTP 409) until the follow-up rebalance has completed. Sink connectors do not need this, because altering consumer group offsets already fails while a sink task'

summary: Producer state snapshot should recover 5 states
GlobalStreamThread runs the uncaught exception handler and its shutdown with the interrupt flag set
body:
Follow-up of KAFKA-21070 (https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23549), as discussed there with [~lucasbru].

The PR for KAFKA-21070 (not merged yet) changes {{StreamThread.run()}} to clear the interrupt flag before the uncaught exception handler and {{completeShutdown}} run, and to restore it when the shutdown is complete. {{GlobalStreamThread}} has its own {{run()}} and does not do this.

If the global thread is interrupted while it is running, the interrupt surfaces as an {{InterruptException}}, for example from the global consumer's {{poll()}}. The constructor of {{InterruptException}} sets the flag again. {{GlobalStreamThread.run()}} catches the exception, calls {{streamsUncaughtExceptionHandler.accept(e)}} and then closes the state consumer in the {{finally}} block, all with the interrupt flag still set:
* The user handler and the state listener run on an interrupted thread.
* The work the handler triggers runs on the interrupted global thread. With a handler that returns {{SHUTDOWN_APPLICATION}} and a single stream thread, {{addStreamThread}} is called from there. In KAFKA-21070 the same call on an interrupted stream thread failed with the streams protocol, in {{ConsumerNetworkThread.start}} on {{initializationLatch.await()}}.
* {{stateConsumer.close(wipeStateStore)}} runs interrupted, so closing the global consumer can be cut short. The state stores are flushed and closed on the interrupted thread as well.

This is from reading the code on trunk. I have not reproduced it for the global thread.

Proposed fix: handle it in {{GlobalStreamThread.run()}} the same way as the PR does in {{StreamThread.run()}}: record and clear the flag in the {{catch}} blocks before the handler runs and once more at the start of the {{finally}} block, and restore it when the shutdown is complete.

summary: setSessionTimeout works incorrectly in ReplicationControlTestContext

summary: Producer sender busy-polls while a partition's head batch is held back by the sequence checks in drain()
body:
When drain() refuses the head batch of a partition for sequencing reasons, ready() has already reported the partition's leader as ready, because readiness only looks at batch size, linger, back-off and the like. Sender.sendProducerData() then sets pollTimeout to 0 because readyNodes is not empty, so the sender loops through ready(), drain() and NetworkClient.poll(0) without sending anything for as long as the partition stays held.

 

Two checks in drainBatchesForOneNode() do this, both only during a leader failover and for at most request.timeout.ms:
 # shouldStopDrainBatchesForPartition(): a retried batch at the head whose sequence is not the first in-flight sequence (trunk today).
 # The hold from KAFKA-18905 (wouldExceedBrokerDeduplicationWindow()): sending one more batch would push the oldest in-flight batch out of the broker's deduplication window.

Measured locally at 2000 records/s with request.timeout.ms=15000: during a 9 s hold the producer JVM used about 0.3 cpu-s per second against 0.1 otherwise, about 600k extra selector polls. Trunk shows the same for case 1 while a leader is SIGSTOPped. Bounded to one partition and one request.timeout.ms, but a busy loop.

Proposed fix: let partitionReady() recognise both conditions and treat the partition as backing off, contributing retry.backoff.ms to nextReadyCheckDelayMs instead of adding the leader to readyNodes. Plain not-ready is not enough: with the old leader's connection black-holed nothing wakes the selector, NetworkClient.poll() only caps its timeout at request.timeout.ms, and the request timeout that releases the hold is detected inside poll(), so the release could lag by up to another request.timeout.ms.

summary: Workflow Requested not working for pull_request_reviewed events
body:
We use the Workflow Requested workflow to automatically approve workflows from the community if the "ci-approved" label is set. 

 

Due to a quirk (deficiency) of the GitHub events schema, there is no easy way to determine the Pull Request for a given workflow. We previously did the following for pull_request events:

 
{code:java}
PR_NUMBER=$(gh api \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  -H "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28" \
  /repos/$REPO/pulls?head=$HEAD_REPO:$HEAD_BRANCH \
  --jq '.[0].number'){code}
 

However, this does not work with pull_request_reviewed events since the HEAD_REPO is set to apache/kafka instead of the PR's origin repository (another annoying "quirk" of the GH API).

 

We need some way to figure out the Pull Request number from a workflow_run "requested" event type. The flow should be:

 
 * pull_request_reviewed is requested due to a review being done
 * Workflow Requested runs, discovers PR number somehow
 * Check PR for "ci-approved" label
 * If label set, approve pending pull_request_reviewed workflow run

summary: Improve new consumer API errors upon background thread failures
body:
The new consumer background thread could fail to start, in which case it will log an error and die. At the moment, the expectation is that consumer api calls will  fail with TimeoutException (KafkaException) when sending events to the background for processing and wait for responses (that will never be received).

We should review to consider improving, given that seems pointless to wait for an event to be processed if we know the background thread is not running. Maybe we can propagate a clearer error message better

 

Note that once in this area, we should also review the errors propagated to the API if the background fails on a single run (runOnce), which also logs but the thread does not die. The expectation in this case is that individual API calls will fail when trying to access resources that may not be available (ex. a request manager). But each process within ApplicationEventProcessor handles this kind of situation differently, so we should improve it if we consider, consistently for all APIs

summary: Authority for LIST_CONFIG_RESOURCES should be dependent upon resource type
body:
KIP-1142 introduced the LIST_CONFIG_RESOURCES RPC as a way of listing Kafka resources for which configuration properties can be described. It built upon KIP-1000 which was specifically concerned with client-metrics resources.
Unfortunately, this RPC requires DESCRIBE_CONFIGS permission on the cluster resource for all resource types. This has the side-effect that you need different permission to list groups (DESCRIBE on CLUSTER) than to list which groups have configs (DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on CLUSTER). This is an unintentional anomaly which leads to incomplete results for the kafka-configs.sh tool for users who only have DESCRIBE authority.
We need a KIP to examine the permissions required for each of the resource types and ensure that there are no such anomalies. Requiring DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the CLUSTER to list client-metrics resources is fine, but it should probably be DESCRIBE on the CLUSTER to list the groups with configs (and then DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the individual groups to describe the actual configs). Similarly, we should make sure that the behavior for topics and so on is sensible.

summary: Infinite loop in MM2 Bi-Directional replication
body:
h3. Background & Problem Statement

In Apache Kafka 3.x, MirrorMaker 2 (MM2) can be configured to use {{IdentityReplicationPolicy}} to preserve original topic names across clusters instead of prefixing them with the source cluster alias (the default behavior in {{{}DefaultReplicationPolicy{}}}).

While {{IdentityReplicationPolicy}} works seamlessly for unidirectional (active-passive) replication, configuring it in a bidirectional (active-active) replication topology ({{{}Cluster A <-> Cluster B{}}}) results in an infinite replication loop:
{noformat}
Cluster A (topic-x) ---> MM2 (A->B) ---> Cluster B (topic-x) ---> MM2 (B->A) ---> Cluster A (topic-x) ...
{noformat}
Because topic names are identical on both clusters and no origin cluster metadata or header check is enforced by default under {{{}IdentityReplicationPolicy{}}}, each MirrorSourceConnector treats replicated records as newly produced local records and replicates them back to the origin cluster indefinitely.
h3. Impact
 * Unbounded message duplication

h3. Steps to Reproduce
 # Configure two Kafka 3.x clusters ({{{}A{}}} and {{{}B{}}}).
 # Configure MirrorMaker 2 with bidirectional flows ({{{}A->B{}}} and {{{}B->A{}}}).
 # Set {{replication.policy.class = org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.IdentityReplicationPolicy}} for both flows.
 # Produce a single message to {{topic-x}} on Cluster {{{}A{}}}.
 # Observe the message continuously cycling between Cluster {{A}} and Cluster {{{}B{}}}.

h3. Expected Behavior / Proposed Enhancement

MirrorMaker 2 should provide a built-in mechanism (such as record header-based origin tracking or explicit loop-detection guardrails/validation) to identify the origin cluster of a message and prevent re-replicating records back to their source cluster—or clearly fail/warn on unsafe bidirectional configurations when using {{{}IdentityReplicationPolicy{}}}.

 

Every events that land on kafka can have a Origin header ,  if mirror maker is trying to replicate to the same kafka cluseter it can drop the message in consumer Interceptor class

 
{code:java}
Cluster A 
    |
Event [ Header {from: A} ]
    |
Mirror Maker (Validate Message is coming from A ( using header ) and going to B - Valid, Replicate )
    |
Cluster B 

---------------

Cluster A 
    |
Event [ Header {from: B} ]
    |
Mirror Maker (Validate Message is coming from A ( using header ) and going to B - Not valid, drop the record)
    |
Cluster B {code}

summary: Streams group heartbeat fails with UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR when a member sets application.server and the group's source topics are missing
body:
If a member of a streams group sends a heartbeat with a user endpoint ({{application.server}}) while the group's configured topology has no subtopologies, the coordinator fails the heartbeat with {{UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR}}. A configured topology has no subtopologies when topic configuration failed, for example because source topics do not exist. In that case the broker should report the missing source topics in the response statuses ({{MISSING_SOURCE_TOPICS}}), which it does for members that do not set an endpoint. The client instead receives {{StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest failed due to unexpected error UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR: null}}, which it treats as fatal, so the application stops instead of waiting for the topics to appear.

On the broker, {{EndpointToPartitionsManager.endpointToPartitions}} calls {{streamsGroup.configuredTopology().flatMap(ConfiguredTopology::subtopologies).get()}}, and that Optional is empty:

{code}
java.util.NoSuchElementException: No value present
  at EndpointToPartitionsManager.endpointToPartitions(EndpointToPartitionsManager.java:74)
  at EndpointToPartitionsManager.maybeEndpointToPartitions(EndpointToPartitionsManager.java:62)
  at StreamsGroup.getOrComputeEndpointToPartitions(StreamsGroup.java:1571)
  at StreamsGroup.buildEndpointToPartitions(StreamsGroup.java:1550)
  at GroupMetadataManager.streamsGroupHeartbeat(GroupMetadataManager.java:2421)
{code}

The failure also hits other members. {{buildEndpointToPartitions}} computes the endpoint mapping for every member of the group, so one member with an endpoint breaks the heartbeats of all of them.

*Steps to reproduce:* start a Kafka Streams application with {{group.protocol=streams}} and {{application.server=host:port}}, using a topology whose source topic does not exist. The {{OrdersService}} example from the Confluent microservices examples does this before its topics are created. The same application without {{application.server}} receives the missing-source-topics status and keeps waiting.

*Expected behaviour:* when the configured topology has no subtopologies, {{buildEndpointToPartitions}} should return an empty list, since there is nothing to map yet, and the heartbeat should return the normal missing-source-topics status.

summary: Add MirrorTopicStateChangeRecord and mirror state tracking in metadata images
body:
KIP-1279 requires the KRaft metadata log to track per-topic mirror state transitions, so that all brokers in the cluster can observe when a topic's desired mirror state changes (e.g. from MIRRORING to PAUSED or STOPPED).

Define a new MirrorTopicStateChangeRecord schema in the metadata module. This record captures the mirror name and the desired mirror state for a given topic, and is written to the metadata log whenever an operator issues a mirror lifecycle command.

Thread mirror state through the existing metadata image/delta pipeline so that mirror name and desired state are available in topic images, replayed correctly through deltas, and surfaced as replica changes for broker-side components to act on.

summary: Consumer fetch metrics are recorded more than once when a fetched partition fails to initialize
body:
{{FetchCollector.initialize()}} reports a partition to {{FetchMetricsAggregator}} in a {{finally}} block, also when it throws. When {{initialize()}} throws, the {{CompletedFetch}} can stay in the {{FetchBuffer}}:

* If the same {{collectFetch()}} call already returned records for another partition, the exception is not thrown and the {{CompletedFetch}} stays in the buffer.
* If the {{CompletedFetch}} still has bytes, it is not removed even when the exception is thrown.

The {{CompletedFetch}} is then reported again by the next {{poll()}}, which calls {{initialize()}} again, or by {{drain()}} when the partition is no longer assigned ({{FetchBuffer.retainAll}}).

{{FetchMetricsAggregator}} records the metrics of the whole fetch response when every partition of the response has reported. After that, each extra report records them again. So, at the client level and the topic level:

* {{records-consumed-total}}, {{records-consumed-rate}}, {{bytes-consumed-total}} and {{bytes-consumed-rate}} are too high.
* {{fetch-size-avg}} and {{records-per-request-avg}} count that response more than once.

Example. One fetch response has two partitions:

* Partition A: 10 records.
* Partition B: {{TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED}}.

# First {{poll()}}: it returns the 10 records of A. B fails to initialize, but the error is not thrown because records were already returned. B stays in the buffer. {{records-consumed-total}} is 10.
# Second {{poll()}}: B fails to initialize again and reports again. The whole response is recorded again. {{records-consumed-total}} is 20. Then {{TopicAuthorizationException}} is thrown.

Expected: {{records-consumed-total}} is 10.

Other errors that can do the same: {{OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE}} without an offset reset policy, and a non-empty partition with no complete record batch.

The same behavior exists in older releases, in {{Fetcher.java}} (checked back to 2.0.0).

Proposed fix: {{FetchMetricsAggregator.record()}} ignores a partition that has already reported.

summary: Flaky test TransactionsWithTieredStoreTest#testRecoveryFromEpochOverflow
body:
TransactionsWithTieredStoreTest#testRecoveryFromEpochOverflow intermittently times out in the second producer's initTransactions(), before the test reaches its epoch rollover assertion.

On trunk revision 53f279fc5882c8644fbf378fea8929852348da6c (macOS, Temurin 25.0.4, Gradle 9.8.2), repetitions 7 and 9 of 10 failed with retries disabled.
{code:bash}
./gradlew :storage:test --rerun --no-parallel --max-workers=3 \
  -PmaxParallelForks=1 -PmaxTestRetries=0 -Pkafka.cluster.test.repeat=10 \
  --tests org.apache.kafka.tiered.storage.integration.TransactionsWithTieredStoreTest.testRecoveryFromEpochOverflow
{code}
In both failures, the helper had set the producer epoch to 32765 while the coordinator was still in PREPARE_ABORT with COMPLETE_ABORT pending. The completion callback carried epoch 1 and threw IllegalStateException. The second producer kept retrying InitProducerId until the test timed out after 60 seconds.

The first abort should complete before the helper sets the boundary epoch. A test-only change waits for COMPLETE_ABORT with no pending transition, then sets the epoch under the same metadata lock. With the original asynchronous send, the tiered and non-tiered tests each passed 10/10 locally. In a separate run with a 750 ms pause before appending the first COMPLETE_ABORT, the original test reproduced the same failure and the changed test passed.

summary: Add MirrorPartition record type
body:
KIP-1279 needs a canonical key type to uniquely identify a mirror partition across the system. Coordinator state lookups, RPC payloads, and partition assignment all reference the same (mirrorName, topicId, partition) triple.

Add a MirrorPartition record in org.apache.kafka.server.mirror within the server-common module. This class will be referenced from multiple modules (core, metadata, mirror-coordinator) and server-common is the lowest common dependency that avoids circular module dependencies.

The record should validate the mirror name (non-empty, max 249 characters, ASCII alphanumeric plus ._-, rejecting "." and "..", following the same constraints as topic names).

summary: Standby task with source-topic changelog fetches and buffers records beyond the committed-offset limit without bound
body:
A standby task whose state store uses the input topic as its changelog may only apply records up to the offset committed by the active task. This happens for {{builder.table(topic)}} when {{topology.optimization}} is set to {{all}} or {{{}reuse.ktable.source.topics{}}}; without this optimization the store has its own changelog topic and is not affected.

{{StoreChangelogReader}} keeps fetching beyond the committed offset, and the records that cannot be applied yet stay in {{{}ChangelogMetadata#bufferedRecords{}}}. Nothing pauses the partition, so the buffer grows with every poll.

When the active task is far behind the end of the input topic, for example when the application starts on a topic that already holds a lot of data, the standby buffers almost the whole backlog and can run out of memory.

Before 2.5.0, {{StreamThread}} paused a standby partition when {{StandbyTask#update}} returned records beyond the offset limit, and resumed it after they were applied. This behavior was lost in the refactoring of KAFKA-9113, so 2.6.0 and later versions are affected.

*Reproduction*
Setup: one broker, two application instances, {{{}num.standby.replicas=1{}}}, {{{}topology.optimization=all{}}}, a topology with {{{}builder.table(inputTopic){}}}, an active task slowed down by a sleep in a downstream processor, and the instance with the standby task in its own JVM with {{{}-Xmx192m{}}}.
 * One input partition, 300,000 records of 1 KB: the standby fails with {{OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space}} after about 5 seconds, with about 139,000 records in the restore buffer.
 * Eight input partitions, 12,000 records of 50 KB (about 600 MB): the standby fails with {{OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space}} after about 8 seconds, with about 2,250 records (about 113 MB) in the restore buffers of its standby partitions.

The same behavior can be shown without an OOM. With {{restore.consumer.max.poll.records=100}} and {{{}commit.interval.ms=100{}}}, the active instance is paused with {{KafkaStreams#pause()}} (so the committed offset does not move) and 10,000 new records are written to the input topic. Within a few seconds the restore consumer of the standby instance fetched 8,703 of them ({{{}records-consumed-total{}}}), although it could not apply any of them.

Other cases do not grow: a standby with its own changelog topic, and an active task that is restoring (records that can be applied are applied right after they are fetched).

*Proposed fix*
Pause such a changelog partition while its buffer holds records beyond the limit offset, and resume it once the limit has moved past them. This restores the behavior from before KAFKA-9113 and adds no new config or public API. The restore buffer then holds at most one poll of records per partition ({{{}max.poll.records{}}}), and the restore consumer keeps at most one fetch per partition (about {{{}max.partition.fetch.bytes{}}}) until the partition is resumed.

The cost: when the committed offset of the active task moves, the standby
comments:

* {{standby-trunk-oom-8-partitions-50kb.log}}: eight input partitions, 12,000 records of 50 KB.

With the fix from the PR, the same run finished all 300,000 records in about 186 seconds, and the standby's heap usage stayed at or below 67 MB.

We can confirm that the described issue also reproduces with Kafka Streams 3.9.2 in our production environment.

Our topology uses a source topic as the changelog for a KTable (reuse.ktable.source.topics), with num.standby.replicas=1. During a large influx of records, active tasks fell behind, while standby tasks continued fetching ahead of the active tasks’ committed offsets. We observed OutOfMemoryError in the StateUpdater thread. Increasing the heap from 1 GiB to 4 GiB and reducing the restore consumer’s max.poll.records and max.partition.fetch.bytes did not prevent subsequent OOMs.

The observed behavior is consistent with the unbounded standby buffering described in this issue, although we have not verified the retained-object ownership through heap dump analysis. We have disabled standby replicas as a temporary workaround.

summary: Verify that `bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets` fails for "streams" group
body:
With KIP-848/1071 we now have three types of groups, "classic", "consumer", and "streams". (And with KIP-932, actually also "share" groups, but they are orthogonal to this ticket).

When users reset group offset, they can use `bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh` tool, which always uses group-type "classic".

For a "consumer" group, this is not a problem, because mixed groups are supported.

However, for a "streams" group, mixed mode (with "classic") is not supported atm. We should add a test that verifies that using `bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh` tool (or actually internally used class), get an error when used for an existing "streams" group.

body:
h3. Summary

Kafka sets fixed socket buffer sizes by default. On Linux, the kernel normally adjusts the buffer size of each TCP connection by itself (this is called auto-tuning). A fixed size turns this off for every Kafka connection. In my test, one consumer reads about 2 times faster when both the broker and the consumer use -1 (about 430 to 600 MB/s with the defaults, about 1000 to 1200 MB/s with -1). With 1 ms of added delay it reads 14 times faster, and with 10 ms 50 times faster. The cost is more kernel memory for connections where the consumer stops reading. I propose to make -1 the default.

h3. Proposal

# Change the defaults in the table in Background to -1.
# Remove {{socket.send.buffer.bytes=102400}} and {{socket.receive.buffer.bytes=102400}} from config/server.properties, config/broker.properties, config/controller.properties and docker/server.properties. These files set the values explicitly, so a change in the code alone does not reach users who start from them.
# Add a note to the upgrade docs.

h3. Background

||Config||Component||Default||
|socket.send.buffer.bytes|broker|102400|
|socket.receive.buffer.bytes|broker|102400|
|replica.socket.receive.buffer.bytes|broker|65536|
|send.buffer.bytes|clients|131072|
|receive.buffer.bytes|consumer, admin client|65536|
|receive.buffer.bytes|producer, Connect, Streams|32768|

Kafka passes these values to {{Socket.setSendBufferSize}} and {{Socket.setReceiveBufferSize}} (SO_SNDBUF and SO_RCVBUF). Without these options, Linux sizes the buffers of each connection by itself, between the limits in the {{tcp_rmem}} and {{tcp_wmem}} sysctls. It grows a buffer when the connection needs it. When an application sets these options, Linux keeps the buffer at that size and does not grow it. (Linux doubles the requested value, so 102400 becomes 204800.) The buffer size limits how much data can be in flight on the connection, so it limits throughput.

All these configs already accept -1 (KAFKA-724, KAFKA-3840 and follow-ups). With -1, Kafka does not call the setters and the kernel sizes the buffers. Some of Kafka's internal clients already use -1: the node-to-controller channel for both buffers, and the KRaft client and the replica fetcher for the send buffer.

The current values do not come from a measurement, as far as I can find. The only documented reason is for the 64 KB consumer default: KAFKA-3463 (2016) set it as a mitigation for KAFKA-3135, which is still open.

h3. Measurement

Kafka trunk (commit e90d6f42c2), one broker (n2-standard-16) and one client (c4-standard-8) in one Google Cloud zone. Linux kernel 7.0.0-1017-gcp (Ubuntu 24.04), with tcp_wmem max 4 MB and tcp_rmem max 32 MB (not changed). One consumer reads a topic with 12 partitions with {{kafka-consumer-perf-test}}. I added delay on the client with {{tc netem}}. Each case has 3 runs. The numbers are the median in MB/s. The first comment has the setup, the commands and more numbers.

||Added delay||Measured round-trip time||Both default|
comments:
h3. Details of the measurement

Setup:
* Kafka trunk at commit e90d6f42c2, JDK 17, Ubuntu 24.04. Kernel 7.0.0-1017-gcp for the runs in the description (the third day); I did not record the kernel version on the first two days.
* Google Cloud, one zone. One broker on n2-standard-16, one client on c4-standard-8.
* Round-trip time about 0.1 to 0.3 ms ({{ping}}; it differs between days). {{iperf3}} with one TCP stream reaches about 30 Gbit/s.
* Kernel limits on the VMs (not changed): tcp_wmem max 4 MB, tcp_rmem max 32 MB.
* One topic, 12 partitions, replication factor 1, 20 GB of 1000-byte records, no compression.
* One consumer, {{group.protocol=consumer}}, 2 GB heap.

Command:
{code}
bin/kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server <broker>:9092 --topic <topic> \
  --num-records 21260087 --command-property group.protocol=consumer \
  --socket-buffer-size 65536
{code}

21260087 records are 99% of the topic. Most runs with added delay used a smaller number.

Note: {{kafka-consumer-perf-test}} sets {{receive.buffer.bytes}} to 2 MB unless {{--socket-buffer-size}} is given. So a run without this option does not show the consumer default. I used {{--socket-buffer-size 65536}} for the default and {{--socket-buffer-size=-1}} for -1.

Results on an earlier day, no added delay (MB/s, 3 runs each):

||Broker socket.send.buffer.bytes||Consumer receive.buffer.bytes||Median||Range||
|102400 (default)|65536 (default)|457|441 to 470|
|102400 (default)|-1|764|717 to 771|
|-1|65536 (default)|449|422 to 467|
|-1|-1|1163|1109 to 1196|

I repeated two of the cases on a second day, with a 30 GB topic. The defaults gave 575 and 593 (2 runs of 15 GB). -1 on both sides gave 1189 (3 runs, 1183 to 1196). The default case differs between days and I do not know why yet. The gain from -1 on both sides is about 2 to 2.5 times on each day. All comparisons in this ticket are between runs on the same day.

What the kernel shows ({{ss -ti}} on the broker, fetch connection):

||Case||Broker send buffer||What the connection waits for||
|Defaults|204800 bytes, fixed|the consumer's receive window ({{rwnd_limited}}) for about 95% of its busy time|
|Broker default, consumer at 2 MB|204800 bytes, fixed|its own send buffer: {{sndbuf_limited}} is about 5% of its busy time and {{rwnd_limited}} is 0|
|Broker at -1, consumer at 2 MB|grows to 4194304 bytes|the receive window for about 30 to 40% of its busy time|

With the consumer at 2 MB, changing only the broker send buffer to -1 raises the throughput from 734 to 1228 MB/s (734 to 1059 in a second set of runs on the same day).

On the consumer side, the receive buffer is fixed at 131072 bytes with the default. With -1 the kernel grows it, and the receive window reached about 17 to 20 MB.

* With the defaults, the consumer's receive buffer is the smaller of the two, so it is the limit.
* Changing only the broker does nothing, because the consumer's receive buffer is still the limit.

summary: Validate Streams task assignor output before accepting target assignments
body:
Streams groups support broker-side custom task assignors. A custom implementation
may return an invalid assignment, but the coordinator currently does not validate several assignment invariants before accepting the result.

No issue has been identified in the built-in sticky assignor. This proposal adds validation to detect invalid output from faulty custom assignors and provide a clear error before that output becomes the group's target assignment.

For example:
 # Member A currently owns task T as active.
 # A custom assignor returns T as active for both A and member B.
 # The coordinator accepts both target assignments.
 # A retains T because it remains in its target assignment.
 # B waits for A to release T.

While A retains ownership and the conflicting target remains unchanged, B cannot
complete reconciliation. The coordinator does not report the invalid assignor
output as the cause.

summary: NamedCache flush cost and heap usage grow with the historical peak of dirty keys
Allow to configure max memory for restore path
body:
Kafka Streams allows users to configure many different memory limits, to pro-actively manage memory usage to avoid OutOfMemory errors.

However, on the restore code path, there is no such memory management. The `StoreChangelogReader` fetches a batch of message, and buffers them inside `ChangelogMetadata`, and there is no limit enforced on this buffer.

We could either re-use the existing config for input topic buffer (`
buffered.records.per.partition`) or introduce a new config (this would require a KIP though). – Even if we re-use the existing config, not 100% sure if we would need a KIP or not?

KIP-1325: [https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-1325%3A+Add+restore.buffered.records.per.partition+to+cap+Kafka+Streams+state-restore+memory]
comments:
Thanks a lot [~mjsax] for taking the time to bring this up. This is based on our observations while 'backfilling' state stores from a huge pile of pre-existing data. Specifically, we are implementing a CDC stack utilizing Debezium and Kafka Streams. Starting the streaming pipeline from scratch means to operate on pre-filled topics with millions of records before regular streaming starts. This backfill phase is extremely difficult to operate because even widely scaled out streams applications frequently die on OutOfMemory errors from restore buffers which can't be effectively controlled resource-wise.

A means to limit memory consumption of the restore path would vastly improve operability in case pipeline restarts are necessary for whichever reason.

I'd be happy to provide additional context or information if needed.

[~mjsax] I tried to look at this. 

So only in the normal processing path, streams enforce a buffer limit via buffered.records.per.partition (default 1000), but when restore happens, there is no such logic in RestoreChangelogReader.

Either we can apply the same config buffered.records.per.partition in RestoreChangelogReader, but 1000 looks low, as it can slow down restoration and we should also consider polling. If polling is faster and restore is slow, we notice a lag.

We can introduce a new config *restore.buffered.records.per.partition* default to a higher default 10000 may be. and the update the [restore()|https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/ccd8330e9eb0e2439f1d025282bef8b724d6ec1d/streams/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/streams/processor/internals/StoreChangelogReader.java#L438] method here

summary: Make the default of receive.buffer.bytes -1 instead of 64k
body:
Currently, kafka has a default config receive.buffer.bytes=64k, which translates to SO_RCVBUF = 65536. As a result, the Linux kernel can't auto tune the receive window. This will cripple performance in many scenarios, especially for internet traffic.

In our environment, we have seen a timeout after [a kernel patch|https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/contributor@example.invalid/T/] that makes the initial receive window 25% instead of 50% of SO_RCVBUF, together with the default request.timeout.ms=30000, it causes an application-level timeout.

See also https://lore.kernel.org/all/contributor@example.invalid/
comments:

Rebalance should be triggered if the subscription is changed during group protocol downgrade triggered by static member replacement
Ensure refiner backward compatibility
body:
We need to ensure that the refiner assigns warm-up task only to new clients, RPC version 1+, but not to old RPC version 0 clients (4.2/4.3 release).

Older clients don't report task-offsets, and thus we cannot use warmup tasks because w/o the ability to observe their restore progress, we could never promote them as active later.

Note one corner case: after a GC fail-over, a member might not have send a heartbeat yet, and thus we don't know it's RPC version yet. Atm, the code treats this incorrectly, and would optimistically assume that it's a v1 client and that we can put warmup task on the client. This must be change to being conservative and treating "unknown" as don't put warmup tasks on the client.

The high level idea is, to add new transient field to `StreamsGroup` to track the RPC version. The tricky part is, that the refiner is computing an intermediate assignment for the whole group, ie, if might be invoked on a v1 heartbeat, that there could still be v0 members in the group. So we could give the individual member's RPC version into the refiner, and the refiner would avoid to put a warmup on older client.
comments: If we treat this conservatively after failover, wouldn't that mean that all task movements are granted after failover, causing unavailability, even if all members are on v1+?

Yes, this would be the fall out for the simple solution of not running the refiner at all. Not sure how often we expect a GC failover, plus having a KS group in the middle of a rebalance at the same time?

For the more complex approach, when we pass in the RPC version for every member into the refiner, the refiner could keep the status quo (ie let the intermediate assignment match the current assignment, including already assigned warm-up tasks) for all members as long as we don't know the version of all members (which is only a small delay of max 2 x heartbeat-interval), and we only start to assign new warm-ups after every member did heartbeat at least once.

summary: Segmented store without segments has no committed offset: task is wiped as corrupted under EOS on every re-initialization
body:
h3. Problem

Under exactly_once_v2, a task that contains a persistent window or session store which holds no segment is treated as corrupted every time the task is initialized on an instance that already has its task directory (after a restart, a rebalance, or a switch between active and standby). The whole task is wiped and restored from the changelogs, including all its other stores. Wiping does not help: the restore re-creates the same empty store directory, so the next initialization fails the same way. A corrupted active task also triggers a rebalance.

A store has no segment when it was never written.
h3. Root cause

* Since KIP-1035 a store keeps its changelog offsets itself. A segmented store keeps them in its segments: {{AbstractSegments#commit}} writes into the existing segments only, and {{AbstractSegments#committedOffset}} returns {{null}} when there are none.
* Opening the store creates its directory ({{AbstractSegments#openExisting}}), so the task directory is not empty afterwards.
* {{ProcessorStateManager#initializeStoreOffsets}} throws {{TaskCorruptedException}} when {{committedOffset}} is {{null}}, EOS is enabled and the task directory was not empty.

A key-value store does not have the problem: it commits the sentinel {{OFFSET_UNKNOWN}} when it has no offset, and {{initializeStoreOffsets}} accepts that.

h3. Reproducer

With {{TopologyTestDriver}} and exactly_once_v2: a topology with a persistent window (or session) store that no processor writes to. Initializing the task on a state directory that contains only the store's empty directory throws:

{noformat}
org.apache.kafka.streams.errors.TaskCorruptedException: Tasks [0_0] are corrupted and hence need to be re-initialized
{noformat}

The same with at_least_once starts normally. The pull request adds this as {{SegmentedStoreWithoutSegmentsTest}}.

h3. Seen in production

A 4-instance application on 4.3.2 with exactly_once_v2, num.standby.replicas=1 and the classic protocol. One sub-topology has a timestamped window store whose changelog is empty on all partitions. After a start with empty state 
directories the group never settled: every probing rebalance (10 minutes apart) ended with tasks of that sub-wiped and restored, on standby and on active tasks, and input lag grew until the application was rolled back to a 4.1  release. No process was killed or restarted during this.

{noformat}
WARN o.a.k.s.p.i.ProcessorStateManager - stream-thread [...] standby-task [2_0] State store <window store> did not find checkpoint offsets while stores are not empty, since under EOS it has the risk of getting uncommitted data in stores we have to treat it as a task corruption error and wipe out the local state of task 2_0 before re-bootstrapping
{noformat}

h3. Proposed fix

Report the committed offset of a segmented store without segments as {{OFFSET_UNKNOWN}}: there is no local data in that state, so nothing can be uncommitted. A store that has a segment but no offset still reports none. {{G
